explanation: Round 1's output was generic and defensive; the diagnosis was thin context (no reason, no new date) and no tone constraint.

question: In that same example, what was diagnosed as still missing after Round 2, which added the cause, new date, and a tone constraint?

options.A: The context was still too thin
options.B: Only the subject line was missing
options.C: The role was undefined
options.D: The task verb was still ambiguous

explanation: Round 2 produced a strong, accountable note; the only remaining gap was the missing subject line.

question: How many rounds did the live iteration cycle example take, and what changed in each round?

options.A: Five rounds, rewriting the entire prompt each time
options.B: Three rounds, each changing exactly the component the previous output exposed
options.C: One round, since the first prompt was already correct
options.D: Ten rounds with random variations

explanation: Three rounds were used, with each round changing exactly the component that the previous round's output had exposed as weak.

question: What signals that iteration has converged and it's time to stop?

options.A: Each additional round produces marginal change rather than improvement
options.B: The output has been rewritten at least five times
options.C: The model tier has been upgraded to Opus
options.D: The user has spent more than ten minutes on the prompt

explanation: Iteration has converged when additional rounds yield only marginal change; at that point, further prompting produces less benefit than a quick manual edit.

question: What is the actual goal of the iteration process, according to the lesson on knowing when to stop?

options.A: A theoretically perfect prompt
options.B: A usable result
options.C: The shortest possible prompt
options.D: A prompt that requires zero human review

explanation: The lesson states explicitly: the goal is a usable result, not a perfect prompt — recognizing diminishing returns is part of the skill.

question: What broader skill, covered in depth in Module 7, uses the same diagnostic discipline as prompt iteration?

options.A: Choosing between model tiers
options.B: Troubleshooting any underperforming workflow
options.C: Setting up Incognito mode
options.D: Creating a new Project from scratch

explanation: The lesson notes that the same diagnostic discipline used in prompt iteration applies to troubleshooting any underperforming workflow, covered in depth in Module 7.

question: A drafted memo came back accurate but far too long and too formal for its audience. What is the most efficient next step?

options.A: Rewrite the entire prompt from scratch
options.B: Switch models and regenerate
options.C: Adjust the constraint and format components (length and tone) and resend
options.D: Manually cut the memo down and abandon the prompt

explanation: Wrong length and tone point specifically to the constraints/format components; adjusting just those and resending is the targeted fix.

question: Why are output deficiencies described as 'prompt diagnostics' rather than simply failures?

options.A: Because each kind of disappointing output points back to a specific, identifiable component gap that can be fixed
options.B: Because Claude labels every output with an error code
options.C: Because the model automatically explains what went wrong
options.D: Because deficiencies always indicate the wrong model tier was used

explanation: Each kind of disappointment (generic output, wrong question answered, wrong length/tone, one weak section) points back to a specific component, making the output itself a diagnostic tool.

question: What is lost when a person discards a mostly-correct draft and starts over with an entirely new prompt after one section falls short?

options.A: Nothing is lost; this is always the most efficient approach
options.B: The parts of the draft that were already working, and the ability to isolate which change fixes the remaining issue
options.C: Only the output format, never the content
options.D: The ability to use Code Execution going forward

explanation: Discarding a mostly-correct draft loses the working parts and removes the ability to identify exactly which change would have fixed the one weak section.

question: Which statement best summarizes the relationship between rewriting and targeted revision?

options.A: They are functionally identical approaches
options.B: Targeted revision changes only the diagnosed component; wholesale rewriting risks losing what already worked and obscures which change caused any improvement
options.C: Wholesale rewriting is always faster and therefore always preferred
options.D: Targeted revision is only possible when using Opus

explanation: Targeted revision isolates and fixes the diagnosed component, while wholesale rewriting risks losing functioning parts of the prompt and obscuring cause and effect.

question: In the live iteration cycle, what was requested as the final Round 3 change?

options.A: A complete rewrite of the email's content
options.B: A subject line that signals resolution, not just delay
options.C: A switch to a more formal tone
options.D: An extension of the word count limit

explanation: Round 3's prompt asked to add a subject line that signals resolution rather than just delay — the one remaining diagnosed gap.

question: What word count constraint was specified in Round 2 of the live iteration example?

options.A: Under 50 words
options.B: Under 120 words
options.C: Under 300 words
options.D: No word limit was specified

explanation: Round 2's prompt specified keeping the note under 120 words, in an accountable, not over-apologetic tone.

question: What does the lesson mean by 'the component stack applies to every prompt, but the emphasis shifts with the task'?

options.A: A different set of components is used for each task type
options.B: The same five components apply everywhere, but which ones need to be tightened versus loosened changes by task type
options.C: Only Analysis and Research use the component stack; Drafting and Brainstorming do not
options.D: The component stack is replaced entirely for creative tasks

explanation: The same five-component stack underlies every prompt; what changes by task type is the balance of specificity versus creative latitude — which components to tighten or loosen.

question: What does Analysis want, in terms of specificity and creative latitude?

options.A: Loose constraints and high creative latitude
options.B: Tight constraints and explicit criteria; low creative latitude, high specification
options.C: No constraints at all, since analysis should be exploratory
options.D: Only a Role component, nothing else

explanation: Analysis wants tight constraints and explicit criteria — what to measure, against what standard, how to handle ambiguity — with low creative latitude and high specification.

question: What does Research want, according to the strategy lesson?

options.A: High creative latitude and loose scope
options.B: Clear scope and source discipline: a defined question, defined boundaries, and clarity on whether current sources are required
options.C: No need to define a question, only a topic
options.D: Exclusively deep multi-source investigation, never quick lookups

explanation: Research wants clear scope and source discipline — the question, the boundaries, and whether current sources are required — with citations requested so claims are checkable.

question: What does Drafting want, in terms of control versus latitude?

options.A: Full control over every word choice, with no latitude at all
options.B: Audience, tone, and format specified, with room for Claude to find the phrasing — medium latitude
options.C: No specification of audience or tone, only a topic
options.D: The same tight constraints as Analysis

explanation: Drafting wants audience, tone, and format specified (medium latitude): the user controls the shape, Claude fills in the phrasing.

question: What does Brainstorming want, according to the strategy lesson?

options.A: Tight constraints and low creative latitude, the same as Analysis
options.B: Loose constraints and high latitude; over-specifying kills the divergence being sought
options.C: No goal statement at all, only constraints
options.D: The exact same treatment as Research

explanation: Brainstorming wants loose constraints and high latitude — give the goal and boundaries, then ask for volume and range before narrowing, since over-specifying kills divergence.

question: In the 'Strategy quick reference' table, what should be tightened for Analysis tasks?

options.A: Word choice
options.B: Criteria, standards, scope
options.C: Quantity and direction
options.D: Synthesis approach

explanation: For Analysis, the table lists criteria, standards, and scope as what to tighten.

question: In the 'Strategy quick reference' table, what should be loosened for Analysis tasks?

options.A: Criteria
options.B: Scope
options.C: Phrasing
options.D: Standards

explanation: For Analysis, phrasing is listed as what to loosen — Claude has latitude in wording even though criteria/standards/scope stay tight.

question: In the 'Strategy quick reference' table, what should be tightened for Research tasks?

options.A: Word choice and tone
options.B: Question, sources, citations
options.C: Quantity and direction
options.D: Goal and guardrails only

explanation: For Research, the question, sources, and citations are what should be tightened.

question: In the 'Strategy quick reference' table, what should be loosened for Research tasks?

options.A: The synthesis approach
options.B: The citation requirement
options.C: The scope of sources allowed
options.D: The definition of the question

explanation: For Research, the synthesis approach is listed as what to loosen, while the question, sources, and citations stay tight.

question: In the 'Strategy quick reference' table, what should be tightened for Drafting tasks?

options.A: Criteria and standards
options.B: Audience, tone, and format
options.C: Goal and guardrails only
options.D: Quantity and direction

explanation: For Drafting, audience, tone, and format are what should be tightened.

question: In the 'Strategy quick reference' table, what should be loosened for Drafting tasks?

options.A: Format
options.B: Tone
options.C: Word choice
options.D: Audience

explanation: For Drafting, word choice is what should be loosened — Claude has room to find the actual phrasing within the specified audience/tone/format.

question: In the 'Strategy quick reference' table, what should be tightened for Brainstorming tasks?

options.A: Criteria, standards, and scope, same as Analysis
options.B: Goal and guardrails only
options.C: Question, sources, and citations
options.D: Audience, tone, and format

explanation: For Brainstorming, only the goal and guardrails should be tightened — everything else stays loose to preserve divergence.

question: In the 'Strategy quick reference' table, what should be loosened for Brainstorming tasks?

options.A: Quantity and direction
options.B: Sources and citations
options.C: Audience and tone
options.D: Criteria and standards

explanation: For Brainstorming, quantity and direction should be loosened, since the goal is a wide range of ideas before narrowing.

question: In the Analysis mini-demo ('Compare these two vendor contracts on payment terms, termination rights, and liability caps...'), what characterizes the prompt?

options.A: Loose criteria and an undefined output shape
options.B: Tight criteria and a defined output (a three-row table), with no room to wander
options.C: An open-ended request with no comparison points specified
options.D: A request for the widest possible range of contract interpretations

explanation: The Analysis demo has tight, named criteria and a clearly defined output shape (a three-row table) — no room to wander.

question: In the Research mini-demo, what is emphasized about citations produced from Claude's training memory alone, versus those from a grounded source?

options.A: They are equally reliable and never need independent verification
options.B: Citations from training memory alone can look equally confident as grounded citations, but should be independently verified
options.C: Training-memory citations are always more accurate than web-search citations
options.D: Citations are never needed for Research tasks

explanation: The lesson explicitly notes that citations produced from training memory alone can look just as confident as grounded ones, and should be independently verified — checkable citations come from a grounded source like web search or Research results.

question: In the Drafting mini-demo ('Draft a 150-word LinkedIn post announcing our new reporting feature, aimed at operations managers, in a confident but not salesy voice'), what is fixed and what is left open?

options.A: Everything is fixed, including exact phrasing
options.B: Audience, length, and tone are fixed; phrasing is left open
options.C: Nothing is fixed; the whole prompt is open-ended
options.D: Only the topic is fixed; everything else is open

explanation: Audience, length, and tone are fixed in the Drafting demo, while the actual phrasing is left open for Claude to determine.

question: In the Brainstorming mini-demo ('Give me 20 angles for a campaign around faster month-end close. Range widely; do not self-edit yet.'), what does this illustrate?

options.A: Tight constraints and low latitude, same as Analysis
options.B: Only the goal and one guardrail are set; constraints come later, after the range exists
options.C: The need for citations and source discipline
options.D: A request for a single best idea to save time

explanation: This demo shows only a goal and one guardrail (range widely, don't self-edit) being set — constraints are deliberately deferred until after the range of ideas exists.

question: What is the risk of using one fixed prompting style across Analysis, Research, Drafting, and Brainstorming tasks?

options.A: There is no risk; one style works equally well for all four
options.B: It costs quality on every task it does not fit
options.C: It only affects Drafting tasks, not the other three
options.D: It automatically triggers a model downgrade

explanation: Using one fixed style across all four task types costs quality on every task it does not fit, since each rewards a different balance of specificity and latitude.

question: A team wants the widest possible range of campaign concepts before narrowing. How should the prompt be calibrated?

options.A: Apply tight constraints on length, format, and terminology up front
options.B: Give the goal and a few guardrails, then ask for volume and range before filtering
options.C: Request a single best idea to save time
options.D: Specify the exact creative direction so Claude stays on message

explanation: This is a Brainstorming task: loose constraints, high latitude — set the goal and guardrails, then ask for volume/range before narrowing.

question: What is the 'underlying move' that stays the same across all four task types, according to the lesson's conclusion?

options.A: Always applying the maximum number of constraints possible
options.B: Deciding where control is needed and where range is needed, then setting constraints accordingly
options.C: Always using Research mode regardless of task type
options.D: Ignoring the component stack for creative tasks

explanation: The lesson concludes that the same underlying move applies every time: decide where you need control and where you need range, then set constraints accordingly.

question: What does the lesson say separates a competent prompter from one who gets the same mediocre output on every task?

options.A: Using the most expensive model tier available
options.B: Matching strategy to task type
options.C: Writing the longest possible prompt every time
options.D: Avoiding the use of constraints entirely

explanation: Matching strategy to task type is explicitly named as what separates a competent prompter from someone who applies one fixed approach and gets mediocre results everywhere.

question: In the checkpoint exercise, the prompt '"Make this better." (pasted alongside a draft email)' is missing which components most obviously?

options.A: Only Role
options.B: Context, Task specificity, Constraints, and Output format are all essentially undefined
options.C: Only Output format
options.D: Nothing is missing; the prompt is complete

explanation: 'Make this better' leaves the task vague, provides no context on what 'better' means, no constraints, and no defined output format.

question: In the checkpoint exercise, the prompt '"Give me everything you know about supply chain risk."' is most clearly missing which component?

options.A: Role only
options.B: Constraints and Task specificity — the request is unbounded with no clear deliverable shape
options.C: Output format only, nothing else
options.D: Context only

explanation: This prompt lacks constraints (scope/boundaries) and a specific task; 'everything you know' is unbounded and produces unfocused output.

question: In the checkpoint exercise, the prompt '"Write a professional document about the project."' most clearly illustrates a gap in which components?

options.A: Role and Constraints only, nothing else
options.B: Context (what project, what audience), Task specificity, and Output format
options.C: Only the Output format is missing
options.D: No components are missing

explanation: 'The project' with no further detail leaves context undefined, the task vague ('a document'), and the output format unspecified.

question: In the checkpoint exercise, the prompt '"Brainstorm names, but each must be one word, under eight letters, avoid these twelve terms, and match our exact brand voice guidelines"' illustrates what kind of problem?

options.A: Missing context only
options.B: Over-constraining a Brainstorming task, which kills the divergence brainstorming is supposed to produce
options.C: A perfectly calibrated prompt with no issues
options.D: Missing Role and Task components

explanation: This over-specifies a Brainstorming task with heavy constraints up front, which — per the Adapting Strategy lesson — undermines the wide range brainstorming is meant to produce.

question: In the 'Repair the Underperforming Prompt' exercise, the weak prompt was 'Summarize the customer feedback and tell me what to do.' What output did it produce?

options.A: A precise, ranked list of the top three issues with representative quotes
options.B: A generic five-bullet list of themes with vague advice, nothing tied to the actual data, no priorities, nothing actionable
options.C: An error message, since the prompt was too short to process
options.D: A fully formatted executive report with citations

explanation: The weak prompt produced generic themes and vague advice, disconnected from the actual data, without priorities or actionable specifics.

question: In that same exercise, what was the author's actual goal?

options.A: A generic overview of customer sentiment with no ranking
options.B: The top three issues by frequency from 200 survey responses, each with a representative quote, ranked so she can decide what to fix this quarter
options.C: A single-sentence summary with no supporting detail
options.D: A comparison of customer feedback against a competitor's feedback

explanation: The product manager's real goal was the top three issues by frequency, each with a representative quote, ranked to inform this quarter's priorities.

question: In that same exercise, which component(s) did the weak prompt fail to specify, based on the gap between the weak output and the stated goal?

options.A: Role and Output format were the only two problems
options.B: Context (the 200 responses and their nature), Task specificity (top three by frequency, ranked), and Output format (quote-supported, ranked list) were all under-specified
options.C: Nothing was missing; the output already matched the goal
options.D: Only the Constraints component was missing

explanation: The weak prompt lacked adequate context about the dataset, a specific enough task (top three by frequency, ranked), and a defined output format (with representative quotes) — all needed to reach the stated goal.

question: In the exercise's fragment-matching stage, which fragment was explicitly identified as 'does not belong' to any of the five components?

options.A: 'You are a product analyst'
options.B: 'Attached are 200 customer survey responses'
options.C: 'Make the summary sound professional and polished'
options.D: 'Format as a ranked list, most frequent first'

explanation: 'Make the summary sound professional and polished' is the fragment that does not map cleanly to Role, Context, Task, Constraints, or Output format — it's vague filler rather than a specification.

question: In the exercise's fragment-matching stage, which fragment best fits the Task component?

options.A: 'You are a product analyst'
options.B: 'Attached are 200 customer survey responses'
options.C: 'Identify the three most frequently raised issues, ranked by how many responses mention each'
options.D: 'Format as a ranked list, most frequent first'

explanation: This fragment states the specific, unambiguous action to perform — identifying and ranking the top three issues — matching the Task component.

question: In the exercise's fragment-matching stage, which fragment best fits the Constraints component, and what does it specify?

options.A: 'You are a product analyst' — specifies the role only
options.B: 'For each issue include one representative verbatim quote and the approximate share of responses it appears in; use code execution to count accurately rather than estimating' — specifies boundaries and a verification requirement
options.C: 'Attached are 200 customer survey responses' — specifies context only
options.D: 'Format as a ranked list, most frequent first' — specifies only the output shape

explanation: This fragment defines boundaries on what to include (a quote, an approximate share) and explicitly constrains the method (use code execution rather than estimating) — a Constraints-type specification.

question: According to Key Takeaway 1 of Module 2, what carries almost every professional prompt?

options.A: Cleverness and creative phrasing
options.B: Five components: role, context, task, constraints, format — run before sending anything that matters
options.C: The choice of model tier alone
options.D: The length of the prompt

explanation: Takeaway 1 states that five components — role, context, task, constraints, format — carry almost every professional prompt and should be run before sending anything that matters.

question: According to Key Takeaway 2 of Module 2, what is the most common cause of generic output?

options.A: A model limitation
options.B: A context gap, not a model limitation
options.C: An overly long prompt
options.D: Using Chat instead of a Project

explanation: Takeaway 2 states that Claude cannot see what lives only in the user's head, and the most common cause of generic output is a context gap, not a model limitation.

question: According to Key Takeaway 3 of Module 2, when do multi-stage requests succeed?

options.A: When they are compressed into a single instruction
options.B: When each step produces a checkable result and the high-stakes foundation is built first
options.C: Only when Research mode is used
options.D: Only when a Project is used instead of Chat

explanation: Takeaway 3 states multi-stage requests succeed when each step produces a checkable result and the high-stakes foundation is built first.

question: According to Key Takeaway 4 of Module 2, how should iteration be approached?

options.A: Rewrite the whole prompt every round regardless of the diagnosis
options.B: Read the output as a diagnostic, change the one thing it points to, and stop when rounds stop improving the result
options.C: Always run at least five iteration rounds regardless of quality
options.D: Iterate only when using the Opus model

explanation: Takeaway 4 states: read the output as a diagnostic, change the one thing it points to, and stop when rounds stop improving the result.

question: According to Key Takeaway 5 of Module 2, what should be decided for each task, and then acted on?

options.A: Which model tier is cheapest
options.B: Where control is needed and where range is needed, then set constraints to fit — since analysis wants constraints and brainstorming wants latitude
options.C: Whether to use Chat or a Project
options.D: Whether Memory should be enabled

explanation: Takeaway 5 states: analysis wants constraints, brainstorming wants latitude — decide where control and where range are needed, then set constraints to fit.

question: A single prompt is used to both decompose a complex vendor evaluation AND apply the wrong task-type strategy (treating it like a Brainstorming task with loose constraints). What would this combination most likely produce?

options.A: A perfectly reasoned, auditable recommendation
options.B: A shallow or unfocused result, since Analysis-type tasks need tight criteria and standards, which loose constraints would undermine
options.C: No output at all, since Claude cannot process mismatched strategies
options.D: The same result as a properly decomposed and correctly calibrated prompt

explanation: Vendor evaluation is an Analysis-type task needing tight criteria/standards; applying loose Brainstorming-style constraints would work against the specificity that task type requires, undermining quality even if decomposed.

question: Which best summarizes the overall throughline connecting the Anatomy of a Prompt, Task Decomposition, Iteration, and Adapting Strategy lessons in Module 2?

options.A: Each lesson is unrelated and covers a completely separate exam domain
options.B: A shared component framework (role, context, task, constraints, format) underlies specification, is applied stage-by-stage in decomposition, is diagnosed and repaired through iteration, and is weighted differently depending on task type
options.C: Only model selection determines prompt quality; the components are optional
options.D: Decomposition and iteration are the same skill taught twice

explanation: The module builds a single coherent framework: the five components define what a good prompt specifies, decomposition applies that framework stage-by-stage to complex tasks, iteration diagnoses and repairs specific component gaps, and task-type strategy adjusts the emphasis placed on each component.

question: The module opens by naming an asymmetry in professional AI use. What is it?

options.A: Errors are large and visible immediately, while the time saved is hidden and hard to measure
options.B: The time saved grows with the length of the output, while the risk of error shrinks
options.C: Verification always costs more time than the drafting it checks
options.D: The time saved is small and visible, while the cost of an unverified error is large and arrives later

explanation: The framing is a small, visible time saving set against a large, delayed cost when an unverified error goes out.

question: In the module's cautionary tale, what happened to the five supporting statistics Claude returned for a client market-sizing deck?

options.A: Four were sound and one growth rate was fabricated; it reached the client deck and was flagged in the room by the client's own analyst
options.B: All five were fabricated, which is why the deck was rejected outright
options.C: The consultant caught the fabricated figure during review, so nothing reached the client
options.D: Claude declined to supply the statistics because no source was connected

explanation: Four figures were sound; one plausible fabricated growth rate survived to the client meeting and was caught by the client's analyst.

question: According to the cautionary tale, when is the cost of a missed error actually paid?

options.A: Only if the error is large enough to be legally actionable
options.B: At the moment the time is saved, which is what makes the trade-off easy to see
options.C: Later, by someone whose trust you need — not at the moment the time is saved
options.D: Never, provided the output came from a high-capability model

explanation: The ten minutes saved cost a credibility hit and a week of rebuilding trust; the bill arrives later and is paid by the relationship.

question: Why does the module say output evaluation is the largest section of the certification exam?

options.A: Because evaluation requires more technical configuration than any other topic
options.B: Accountability — when you put your name on a deliverable you own every claim in it, whether you wrote the words or Claude did
options.C: Because hallucination is the only failure mode Claude exhibits
options.D: Because the exam weights each section by how many product features it covers

explanation: The stated reason is accountability: ownership of every claim in anything you ship.

question: How is the Discernment competency defined in this module?

options.A: The habit of making each prompt component explicit rather than assuming inference
options.B: The skill of deciding when verification is required and taking responsibility for the result
options.C: The skill of critically evaluating output against requirements, sources, and standards
options.D: The practice of choosing the entry point before writing the prompt

explanation: Discernment is critical evaluation against requirements, sources, and standards — it is how you review.

question: How is the Diligence competency defined in this module?

options.A: Critically evaluating output against requirements, sources, and standards
options.B: Deciding when verification is required and taking responsibility for the result
options.C: Splitting a multi-part request into discrete, ordered steps
options.D: Reviewing stored memories on a regular cadence and deleting expired entries

explanation: Diligence is deciding when verification is required and owning the result — it is why you must review.

question: Which of the following is NOT one of the module's stated learning objectives?

options.A: Configure account-level Memory so verification results persist across every future session
options.B: Identify hallucinations, inconsistencies, and biases in output
options.C: Determine when human review or additional verification is required
options.D: Select appropriate output formats and organize information for optimal results

explanation: Memory configuration belongs to Module 1's capability layer; it is not among this module's six objectives.

question: How does the lesson define evaluation?

options.A: A comparison of two Claude outputs to see which one reads better
options.B: An intuition that sharpens with experience and eventually replaces formal checks
options.C: A single pass to confirm the output answers the question that was asked
options.D: Not a feeling about whether output looks good, but a check against three fixed references

explanation: Evaluation is a repeatable check against three fixed references, run the same way every time.

question: What are the three evaluation references in the Discernment protocol?

options.A: Requirements, model tier, and output format
options.B: Accuracy, completeness, and formatting
options.C: Stakes, reversibility, and audience
options.D: Requirements, source material, and professional standards

explanation: The three references are the requirements you set, the source material you supplied, and the professional standards of your field.

question: What does checking output against the Requirements reference involve?

options.A: Comparing the output against a previous output on the same topic
options.B: Asking Claude to restate the request to confirm it understood
options.C: Re-reading your own request and confirming each part is addressed, not just the easy parts
options.D: Confirming the output is formatted the way your team prefers

explanation: The requirements check is a re-read of your own request, part by part, including the parts that were harder to satisfy.

question: What does the Source material reference require when the output relies on documents you supplied?

options.A: Re-uploading the documents and running the same prompt a second time
options.B: Tracing specific claims back to the source rather than trusting that Claude read carefully
options.C: Checking that the output cites the same number of documents you uploaded
options.D: Confirming the summary is shorter than the source material

explanation: Specific claims get traced back to the document; you do not assume careful reading on Claude's part.

question: Which of these is given as an example of failing professional standards even when the output reads fluently?

options.A: A number without units, a recommendation without reasoning, or a citation you cannot locate
options.B: An output that is longer than the request implied
options.C: An output that uses bullet points where prose was expected
options.D: An output produced on a lower model tier than the task warranted

explanation: These three all read fluently and all fail the standards of a professional field.

question: Why does the lesson insist on running the same check the same way every time?

options.A: Because a varied review process consumes more of the usage limit
options.B: Because Claude produces identical output whenever a check is repeated
options.C: Because the exam requires the three references to be checked in a fixed order
options.D: So quality does not depend on how rushed you happen to be

explanation: A fixed protocol keeps review quality from tracking your available time and attention.

question: According to stakes calibration, how universal are review stakes?

options.A: They depend only on the length of the output
options.B: They are universal: every output deserves the same depth of review
options.C: They are domain-dependent, not universal — depth of review follows what is at stake in that field
options.D: They depend on which model tier produced the output

explanation: Stakes are domain-dependent, so the depth of review is calibrated to the domain rather than applied uniformly.

question: In zero-tolerance work such as legal analysis, financial figures, and compliance reporting, what does the lesson prescribe?

options.A: Accuracy takes priority over speed entirely, and every claim gets verified
options.B: A lighter review, since these domains have external safeguards of their own
options.C: The same review depth as internal brainstorming, simply carried out faster
options.D: Verification of the formatting only, since the figures come from source documents

explanation: In zero-tolerance domains accuracy outranks speed and every claim is verified.

question: What risk does the stakes-calibration section name?

options.A: Spending too long reviewing internal brainstorming output
options.B: Applying the same casual review to high-stakes and low-stakes work alike
options.C: Reviewing regulated work twice, which duplicates effort
options.D: Choosing an output format before the stakes are known

explanation: A lighter review suits low-stakes internal work; the risk is carrying that same casual review into work where it does not belong.

question: What are the three verdicts in the module's output triage?

options.A: Accurate, incomplete, unfit
options.B: Ready to use, needs revision, needs human override
options.C: Ship, iterate, discard
options.D: Low stakes, medium stakes, high stakes

explanation: Each output is sorted into one of these three states, with the reasoning documented.

question: Under the triage, when does an output qualify as 'needs revision'?

options.A: Any output that has not yet been read from beginning to end
options.B: The stakes or the uncertainty mean it should not go out on Claude's draft alone
options.C: It meets requirements, matches sources, and clears professional standards
options.D: It is close, but a specific gap remains — note the gap and iterate

explanation: 'Needs revision' is the verdict when the output is close and the remaining gap is specific and nameable.

question: When does an output need human override?

options.A: Whenever the output was produced without web search enabled
options.B: Whenever a single formatting inconsistency appears anywhere in the output
options.C: When the stakes, the errors, or the uncertainty mean it should not go out on Claude's draft alone
options.D: Whenever one round of iteration has already been attempted

explanation: Human override is escalation to a person, triggered by stakes, error load, or uncertainty.

question: What does the 'ready to use' verdict require?

options.A: It meets the requirements, matches the sources, and clears professional standards
options.B: It reads fluently and contains no obvious errors
options.C: It was produced from documents the user uploaded personally
options.D: It has been through at least three rounds of iteration

explanation: All three references have to clear before an output ships without further work.

question: How do accuracy and completeness differ, and how do they fail?

options.A: Completeness is a subset of accuracy, so an accurate output is complete by definition
options.B: Accuracy asks whether what is present is correct; completeness asks whether anything is missing — and they fail independently
options.C: They always fail together, which is why a single check covers both
options.D: Accuracy applies to numbers and completeness applies to prose

explanation: An output can be entirely accurate and still omit the one factor that changes a decision.

question: Why are missing elements harder to spot than wrong ones?

options.A: Because completeness can only be assessed by a second reviewer
options.B: Because Claude deliberately omits material it has low confidence in
options.C: Because omissions only occur in outputs longer than one page
options.D: Nothing on the screen draws your eye to something that is absent

explanation: Wrong content is visible; absent content has nothing on the page to catch your attention.

question: In the worked protocol, Claude summarized three competitors' published pricing from uploaded PDFs. Requirements were met, but the source review caught a problem. What was the verdict?

options.A: Needs human override — pricing comparisons always require escalation
options.B: Ready to use — all three competitors were covered as requested
options.C: Needs revision — and the fix is a source-matched re-prompt, not a rewrite
options.D: Ready to use, provided the PDFs are re-uploaded first

explanation: A specific, traceable source mismatch is exactly the 'needs revision' case; the repair is targeted, not a fresh start.

question: What did the source review catch in that competitor-pricing summary?

options.A: Each tier was listed as '$40/user' when the uploaded PDF said '$40/user, minimum 10 seats,' which changes the comparison
options.B: One competitor had been omitted from the summary entirely
options.C: The summary invented a fourth competitor that was not in the PDFs
options.D: The prices were correct but presented in the wrong currency

explanation: The dropped seat minimum is a source-fidelity failure that materially changes the comparison.

question: You asked for three options to reduce invoice-processing time and received three sensible options with trade-offs — an internal discussion starter, with no sources to check against. What is the verdict and why?

options.A: Needs human override — process recommendations affect how the team operates
options.B: Needs revision — any output without citations requires a grounded re-prompt
options.C: Ready to use — over-verifying this one wastes the time the tool saved
options.D: Ready to use, but only after the figures are recomputed with code execution

explanation: Requirements met, no sources to check, standards cleared, low stakes: verifying further would spend the saving for nothing.

question: Claude compared your data-handling policy against a regulation and confidently flagged four gaps — but the regulation itself was never uploaded. What is the verdict?

options.A: Ready to use — four flagged gaps is a substantive, actionable result
options.B: Needs human override — Claude worked from training-data recall of a rule that may have changed, and the stakes are regulatory
options.C: Needs revision — asking Claude to double-check its own four gaps resolves the issue
options.D: Ready to use, provided the output is relabeled as a draft

explanation: The output is a useful prompt for a compliance expert, not a substitute for one.

question: Why can tone or confidence not be used to flag an error in Claude's output?

options.A: Claude writes fluently whether it is right or wrong, so plausible is not the same as verified
options.B: Because Claude hedges more heavily when it is uncertain, which masks the real errors
options.C: Because confidence is only an unreliable signal on lower model tiers
options.D: Because tone varies at random between runs and therefore carries no information of any kind

explanation: Fluency is constant regardless of correctness, so it cannot serve as an error signal.

question: What is the practical benefit of learning the specific signatures of failure?

options.A: You can identify which model tier produced a given error
options.B: You can stop reviewing outputs once you recognize the patterns reliably
options.C: You can delegate the review to Claude by naming the patterns in the prompt
options.D: You can spot failures quickly instead of reading every line with equal suspicion

explanation: Pattern recognition makes review fast and targeted rather than uniformly slow.

question: Why are plausible-but-unsupported claims described as the most dangerous hallucination pattern?

options.A: They appear only in long outputs, where reviewers stop reading carefully
options.B: They are always attached to fabricated citations, which take time to check
options.C: They sound reasonable and fit the topic, and nothing about them looks wrong
options.D: They cause Claude to contradict itself later in the same output

explanation: The danger is the absence of any surface signal: the claim has no basis in the source or in fact, and still reads normally.

question: Why are fabricated specifics — invented statistics, dates, names, quotations, or citations — so persuasive?

options.A: They are usually correct, which is what makes the rare exceptions dangerous
options.B: Specificity reads as authority, which is exactly why an invented precise detail convinces
options.C: They always arrive with a hedge that reviewers tend to overlook
options.D: They only appear when the prompt explicitly asks for numbers

explanation: Precision looks like evidence, so a fabricated specific carries more weight than a vague claim would.

question: What does 'confident tone masking uncertainty' mean?

options.A: Claude rarely hedges in proportion to its actual certainty; a guess and a well-grounded fact arrive in the same assured voice
options.B: Claude signals its uncertainty clearly, but reviewers routinely ignore the signal
options.C: Claude hedges on everything, so hedging carries no information
options.D: Claude's tone becomes noticeably less confident as its accuracy drops

explanation: Hedging does not track certainty, so the voice is the same whether the claim is grounded or guessed.

question: Where do internal contradictions most often hide, and why?

options.A: In the opening paragraph, which reviewers tend to skim
options.B: In short outputs, where each individual claim carries more weight
options.C: In tables, because numbers are harder to read than prose
options.D: In long documents, because you rarely hold the whole thing in view at once

explanation: Length is what conceals a contradiction: claims made early can conflict with claims made later.

question: What is confirmation bias in framing?

options.A: Claude reuses the same framing across separate conversations
options.B: Claude systematically disagrees with the premise of any leading question
options.C: If your prompt implies a preferred answer, Claude may lean toward it — so watch for output that agrees with you too readily on a genuinely open question
options.D: Claude favors whichever source appears earliest in an uploaded document

explanation: A leading prompt can pull the answer with it, which is most dangerous when the question was supposed to be open.

question: A professional asked Claude to compare a batch of documents and identify the differences. The output read as thorough but missed the differences in the single most important file. What is the lesson?

options.A: Completeness failures concentrate where attention is lowest, and a confident summary of the easy files can mask silence on the hard one
options.B: Claude cannot compare more than two documents in a single request
options.C: Batch comparisons should always be run on a higher model tier
options.D: The output was inaccurate rather than incomplete, since the listed differences were wrong

explanation: The listed differences were fine; the failure was the silence on the file that mattered most.

question: Claude states 'I've emailed this to your team' or 'I've saved the file.' How should such a claim be treated?

options.A: As reliable, since Claude would not report an action it had not taken
options.B: As unverified — Claude does not perform external actions it was not given a tool for, so confirm the action actually happened
options.C: As a formatting artifact with no bearing on the content of the output
options.D: As evidence that a connector was enabled earlier in the session

explanation: This is a capability hallucination: within claude.ai Claude works with the conversation, connected tools, and uploaded files, and any other claimed action needs confirming.

question: An output reads: 'Approximately 63 percent of mid-market SaaS firms adopted at least one AI tool in 2025, up from 41 percent in 2024,' with no source given. What is the tell?

options.A: The subject matter, since Claude has no knowledge of SaaS markets at all
options.B: The hedge 'approximately,' which signals Claude knew it was uncertain
options.C: The two-year comparison, which Claude is unable to compute
options.D: The precision — real figures this specific arrive with a citation, so an unsourced 63 percent is a number-shaped guess

explanation: Specificity without a citation is the signature of a fabricated specific.

question: Asked whether a clause is enforceable in your state, Claude gives a four-sentence answer stating that it is, in the same assured voice it uses for arithmetic. What is the problem?

options.A: Claude should never be asked about contract clauses in any form
options.B: The answer is too short to be trustworthy, since length signals depth of analysis
options.C: Enforceability is jurisdiction-specific and date-sensitive — exactly the kind of claim that should hedge and does not; assurance is not evidence
options.D: The answer used prose where a structured format was required

explanation: The claim type demands hedging and citation; the confident tone is the failure signature, not a reassurance.

question: In a ten-page market analysis, page two states the addressable market is 'roughly $2 billion' while page eight builds a projection on 'the $2.6 billion market.' What does this illustrate?

options.A: A paragraph-by-paragraph read is sufficient provided it is done slowly enough
options.B: Claude cannot handle figures above one billion reliably
options.C: The projection is wrong and the earlier figure is right, so page eight should simply be deleted
options.D: Long outputs need a consistency pass across the whole document, because both statements read fine in isolation

explanation: Neither page looks wrong on its own; only a whole-document consistency pass surfaces the conflict.

question: Why is a careful paragraph-by-paragraph read insufficient for catching internal contradictions?

options.A: Because contradictions are typically placed in footnotes
options.B: Each claim is individually plausible; the conflict is only visible when the whole document is held in view
options.C: Because reading order changes the meaning of each paragraph
options.D: Because Claude marks contradictions only in the closing summary

explanation: Contradiction is a relationship between distant claims, so local reading cannot detect it.

question: How does the lesson say the failure-pattern gallery should be read?

options.A: None of the outputs looks broken — you catch these by knowing the signatures and checking against sources, not by waiting for something to look wrong
options.B: Each example contains a visible error that a careful reader will notice
options.C: The gallery shows failure modes unique to older model versions
options.D: The gallery is illustrative only; these patterns are rare in real work

explanation: Fluent generation is designed to pass a casual read, so detection comes from signatures and sources rather than from an output looking off.

question: Where does the lesson say the strongest verification lives?

options.A: In a second review pass by a colleague after delivery
options.B: Built into the prompt, before the output exists
options.C: In the model tier selected for the task
options.D: In a line-by-line fact-check of everything produced

explanation: Prompt-level habits cut hallucinations at the source rather than catching them afterward.

question: Why tell Claude explicitly that admitting uncertainty is acceptable?

options.A: Without that permission, a model under pressure to answer is more likely to fill the gap with something invented
options.B: Because Claude cannot produce the phrase 'I don't know' unless the prompt contains it
options.C: Because it shortens the output, which reduces the review burden
options.D: Because it switches Claude into a grounded retrieval mode automatically

explanation: Permitting 'I don't know' removes the pressure that produces invented filler.

question: What does restricting Claude to provided sources accomplish?

options.A: It prevents Claude from reformatting the source documents
options.B: It guarantees the output will contain no errors of any kind
options.C: It converts open-ended generation into bounded retrieval, with anything the materials do not cover flagged rather than filled in
options.D: It removes the need to review the output before use

explanation: The instruction bounds the answer to the supplied material and turns gaps into flags.

question: What makes a citation auditable?

options.A: It was produced in a session where web search had been enabled at some point
options.B: It names a well-known publication, which establishes credibility
options.C: It appears in a footnote rather than inline
options.D: It gives the specific source and location behind the claim, in a form you can check

explanation: A citation you cannot trace is not a citation; the location has to be checkable.

question: The verification checklist asks four questions before you rely on an output. Which set?

options.A: Did I pick the right entry point, the right model, the right Skill, and the right format?
options.B: Did I allow uncertainty, restrict to sources where appropriate, require citations I can audit, and check the high-stakes claims against something authoritative?
options.C: Is it accurate, is it complete, is it well formatted, and is it on time?
options.D: Did I define the role, the context, the task, and the constraints?

explanation: These four questions are the module's pre-reliance checklist.

question: Why does the lesson argue for prevention over after-the-fact correction?

options.A: Building these habits into the prompt is cheaper than rebuilding trust in the output afterward
options.B: Because errors caught after the fact cannot be corrected
options.C: Because post-hoc checks are only available on paid plans
options.D: Because Claude cannot revise an output once it has been produced

explanation: The cost compared is prompt-time effort versus the far larger cost of repairing trust later.

question: You need Claude to answer questions strictly from a contract you uploaded, without inventing anything. Which prompt technique most reduces hallucination?

options.A: Use the most capable model and ask in a single sentence
options.B: Ask the question and trust Claude to stay within the document
options.C: Ask the same question five times and average the answers
options.D: Restrict the answer to the provided document, permit 'I don't know,' and require citations to specific clauses

explanation: All three grounding habits apply together: bounded sources, permitted uncertainty, and clause-level citations.

question: A researcher asks for market statistics and receives five precise figures with no citations. Which prompt habit would most likely have prevented this?

options.A: Asking for ten figures so the weakest ones stand out by comparison
options.B: Requesting a table instead of prose so the figures are easier to read
options.C: Requiring auditable citations — the specific source and location for each figure — and permitting 'I don't know'
options.D: Raising the model tier and rerunning the identical prompt

explanation: Unsourced precise figures are the fabricated-specific pattern; the citation requirement is the direct preventive habit.

question: What is the purpose of instructing Claude to flag anything the supplied materials do not cover?

options.A: It causes Claude to search the web for the missing material automatically
options.B: It shortens the output by omitting any uncovered topic
options.C: It surfaces the gaps explicitly instead of letting generation quietly fill them
options.D: It shifts responsibility for the gaps onto the source documents

explanation: Flagged gaps are visible and reviewable; unflagged gaps get filled with plausible invention.

question: Which of the following is NOT one of the lesson's prompt habits for reliability?

options.A: Run the prompt several times and average the numeric answers so errors cancel out
options.B: Permit 'I don't know' explicitly
options.C: Restrict the answer to the sources you provided
options.D: Require citations you can audit

explanation: Averaging repeated generations is not a grounding technique; the three habits are permitted uncertainty, restricted sources, and auditable citations.

sectionTitle: Diligence: When Human Review Is Non-Negotiable
question: What does Diligence mean in this module?

options.A: Reviewing every output to the same depth regardless of what is at stake
options.B: Knowing the escalation thresholds in advance, so the decision to escalate is made by policy rather than in the moment after something has gone wrong
options.C: Iterating on a prompt until the output stops changing between rounds
options.D: Recording which model tier produced each deliverable

explanation: Diligence sets the thresholds in advance so escalation is a policy decision, not an improvisation under pressure.

sectionTitle: Diligence: When Human Review Is Non-Negotiable
question: What are the four risk thresholds?

options.A: Cost, speed, volume, and model tier
options.B: Accuracy, completeness, clarity, and tone
options.C: Requirements, sources, standards, and format
options.D: Stakes, reversibility, audience, and regulatory exposure

explanation: These four questions decide whether human review is mandatory.

sectionTitle: Diligence: When Human Review Is Non-Negotiable
question: Which question belongs to the Stakes threshold?

options.A: Does a rule, contract, or law govern this content?
options.B: Can the action be undone once it has been taken?
options.C: Who sees it — internal, external, executive, or regulatory?
options.D: What is the cost if this is wrong? High-cost errors demand human review regardless of how confident the output appears

explanation: Stakes asks about the cost of being wrong, independent of how the output reads.

sectionTitle: Diligence: When Human Review Is Non-Negotiable
question: Which question belongs to the Reversibility threshold?

options.A: Which audience will ultimately read the output?
options.B: What is the cost if the output turns out to be wrong?
options.C: Can the action be undone? An irreversible step, such as a sent client deliverable or a filed report, clears a higher bar than a draft you can revise
options.D: Is the content governed by a regulation or a contract?

explanation: Reversibility asks whether the step can be walked back; irreversible steps carry a higher review bar.

sectionTitle: Diligence: When Human Review Is Non-Negotiable
question: Which question belongs to the Audience threshold?

options.A: How long will the output remain in circulation?
options.B: Who sees it? External, executive, and regulatory audiences raise the review requirement above internal working drafts
options.C: Can the deliverable be recalled after it has been sent?
options.D: Does the output contain figures that need recomputing?

explanation: Audience raises or lowers the bar: internal drafts sit below external, executive, and regulatory readers.

sectionTitle: Diligence: When Human Review Is Non-Negotiable
question: Which question belongs to the Regulatory exposure threshold?

options.A: Does a rule, contract, or law govern this? Regulated content carries obligations that AI assistance does not remove
options.B: Is the reviewer qualified to interpret the regulation in question?
options.C: Has the regulation been uploaded to the Project knowledge base?
options.D: Will the output be read by more than one person?

explanation: Regulated content carries obligations that using an AI tool does not remove or transfer.

sectionTitle: Diligence: When Human Review Is Non-Negotiable
question: Which of the following belongs on the do-not-ship-without-review list?

options.A: Final client deliverables, audit-critical or financially material calculations, regulated or highly sensitive data, and public or legal communications
options.B: Any output longer than two pages, regardless of its content
options.C: Any output produced in a session where code execution was disabled
options.D: Internal meeting agendas and early-stage brainstorms

explanation: These four categories are the fixed list, decided in advance.

sectionTitle: Diligence: When Human Review Is Non-Negotiable
question: How should the do-not-ship-without-review list be treated?

options.A: Applied only when the output contains numbers
options.B: Revisited for each deliverable, since the categories shift with workload
options.C: Decided in advance and treated as fixed, so the escalation call is never made under time pressure
options.D: Delegated to Claude, which can classify outputs against the list

explanation: The point of a fixed list is that the judgment is already made before the deadline arrives.

sectionTitle: Diligence: When Human Review Is Non-Negotiable
question: What distinguishes productive iteration from the point where escalation is required?

options.A: Escalation is required whenever the model tier changes mid-task
options.B: Iteration is productive through the fifth round, after which escalation is automatic
options.C: Escalation is required only once a visible error appears in the output
options.D: Productive iteration improves the output each round; when rounds stop improving it, the right move is human review rather than another prompt

explanation: Diminishing returns is the signal: the next move is a person, not another prompt.

sectionTitle: Diligence: When Human Review Is Non-Negotiable
question: What does the lesson mean by saying more prompting cannot manufacture the judgment a situation requires?

options.A: Prompt quality has no effect on output quality in high-stakes work
options.B: Some situations need a person's judgment, and no further round of prompting substitutes for it
options.C: Judgment can be encoded in a prompt if the constraints are precise enough
options.D: Iteration should be avoided entirely on any task with external stakes

explanation: Recognizing that line — where prompting stops and judgment starts — is part of Diligence.

sectionTitle: Diligence: When Human Review Is Non-Negotiable
question: What does the module say about owning the output?

options.A: Accountability passes to the reviewer once the output has been escalated
options.B: Accountability is shared between the user and the model provider
options.C: Accountability does not transfer to the tool — work produced with Claude is your work when you ship it, held to the same standard as unaided work
options.D: Accountability applies only to outputs that leave the organization

explanation: The professional standard is identical to work produced without assistance; Diligence is the habit of acting as though that is true.

sectionTitle: Diligence: When Human Review Is Non-Negotiable
question: Claude drafts an internal meeting agenda. How do the four thresholds resolve?

options.A: Low stakes, reversible, internal audience, no regulatory exposure — the routine case you can move quickly on
options.B: Low stakes but irreversible, so a second reader is still required
options.C: Internal audience but high regulatory exposure, so escalation applies
options.D: All four thresholds are ambiguous, so the default is human override

explanation: This is the fast 'yes': all four thresholds sit low, so the routine path is appropriate.

sectionTitle: Diligence: When Human Review Is Non-Negotiable
question: Claude produces a board-deck financial summary that reads cleanly. What does the module prescribe?

options.A: The clean appearance is evidence the figures are sound, so it can ship as drafted
options.B: It trips three thresholds — high stakes, executive audience, partly irreversible once presented — so it goes to a human reviewer and the figures get recomputed with code execution
options.C: It should be rerun on a higher model tier and then shipped
options.D: Only the formatting needs review, since the figures came from Claude's own calculation

explanation: This is the deceptive 'looks fine': the clean surface is irrelevant to the three thresholds it trips.

sectionTitle: Diligence: When Human Review Is Non-Negotiable
question: You have iterated a client proposal five times, and rounds three through five changed almost nothing. What is the signal, and what should you do?

options.A: Restart the task in a fresh conversation and run five more rounds
options.B: The absence of any visible error is the signal that the proposal is ready to send
options.C: Five rounds is the maximum, so the fifth version should go out as it stands
options.D: The flat improvement curve is the signal — stop prompting and escalate to a colleague for a fresh read

explanation: This is the slow creep: diminishing returns on a high-stakes external deliverable calls for a human, not another round.

sectionTitle: Editing and Adapting Output for Your Audience
question: 'Claude drafts; you deliver.' What does the editing pass apply?

options.A: The formatting rules attached to the output modality you selected
options.B: A second model's judgment about which draft reads better
options.C: Your professional standards and your knowledge of the audience
options.D: The verification checklist, which replaces the need to edit

explanation: The editing pass is where your standards and your audience knowledge enter the deliverable.

sectionTitle: Editing and Adapting Output for Your Audience
question: What does 'a draft that is accurate is still not finished' mean?

options.A: Editing becomes optional once the facts have been verified
options.B: Accuracy cannot be established until after editing is complete
options.C: An accurate draft only needs a formatting change to be finished
options.D: Accuracy is necessary but not sufficient; the gap between a raw draft and a finished deliverable is the editing pass

explanation: Verification and editing are separate passes; clearing one does not clear the other.

sectionTitle: Editing and Adapting Output for Your Audience
question: What are the three passes that turn a raw draft into a deliverable?

options.A: Clarity, tone, and formatting
options.B: Accuracy, completeness, and fitness
options.C: Requirements, sources, and standards
options.D: Inline, artifact, and structured

explanation: Three passes: clarity, tone, and formatting.

sectionTitle: Editing and Adapting Output for Your Audience
question: What does the clarity pass involve?

options.A: Adding detail wherever the draft is thin, since thoroughness signals rigor
options.B: Cutting hedging and tightening loose sentences — Claude tends toward thoroughness, while editing tends toward precision
options.C: Matching the register to the relationship and the occasion
options.D: Shaping the output for the way it will be read

explanation: Clarity removes anything that does not earn its place, pulling a thorough draft toward precision.

sectionTitle: Editing and Adapting Output for Your Audience
question: What does the tone pass involve?

options.A: Matching the register to the relationship and the occasion — the same content reads differently to a peer, a client, and a regulator
options.B: Adopting a uniformly formal register for every audience to stay safe
options.C: Preserving Claude's original phrasing so the draft stays internally consistent
options.D: Removing every sentence that does not earn its place

explanation: Tone is register calibration, not a fixed level of formality.

sectionTitle: Editing and Adapting Output for Your Audience
question: What does the formatting pass involve?

options.A: Matching the format to the model tier that produced the draft
options.B: Applying the same template to every deliverable for consistency
options.C: Converting every deliverable into a structured table
options.D: Shaping the output for how it will be read: scannable for an executive, detailed for a working team, clean for an external recipient

explanation: Formatting follows the reading situation, not a house template.

sectionTitle: Editing and Adapting Output for Your Audience
question: One analysis often has to become several deliverables. How do the versions differ?

options.A: Only the length changes; selection and tone stay fixed
options.B: Each version restates a different set of facts drawn from the same analysis
options.C: The underlying facts hold steady while selection, depth, and tone change — executives get decision and impact, working teams get detail and method, external communications control disclosure and framing
options.D: The executive version carries the most detail, since executives make the decisions

explanation: Facts are constant; what varies is what is selected, how deep it goes, and how it is framed.

sectionTitle: Editing and Adapting Output for Your Audience
question: What does the lesson recommend before you start editing, when quality matters?

options.A: Commit to the first response, since comparison introduces inconsistency
options.B: Generate more than once, or across models, and choose the strongest base to edit from rather than committing to the first response
options.C: Ask Claude which of its own drafts is strongest and edit that one
options.D: Compare drafts only when the first one contains a factual error

explanation: Comparing candidates is cheaper than reworking a weak draft, and it exposes framings you might not have prompted for.

sectionTitle: Editing and Adapting Output for Your Audience
question: In the worked transformation, a raw draft on Q3 processing time became an executive version and a working-team version. What stayed the same?

options.A: The facts, including the same 18 percent — only selection, depth, and tone changed
options.B: The sentence structure, which was preserved in both versions
options.C: The length, since both versions had to fit the same space
options.D: Nothing; each version reported a different figure suited to its audience

explanation: Same facts, same 18 percent; the two cuts differ in what they keep and how they frame it.

sectionTitle: Editing and Adapting Output for Your Audience
question: In that transformation, what does each cut do?

options.A: The executive cut adds method, while the working cut removes it
options.B: The executive cut strips method and leads with impact; the working cut keeps the method and assigns an action with an owner and timeline
options.C: Both cuts drop the recommendation and report only the figure
options.D: The working cut is simply a shortened version of the executive cut

explanation: Neither is a raw draft, and neither version would serve the other audience.

sectionTitle: Choosing Output Formats: Inline, Artifacts, Structured, Code-Executed
question: How does the lesson frame the choice of output format?

options.A: As a consequence of the model tier selected for the task
options.B: As a presentation choice that follows the reader's stated preference
options.C: As a reliability decision, not just a presentation choice — driven by what the result is for and how much the numbers have to be trusted
options.D: As a setting that should stay constant across a workstream

explanation: Format is chosen by the reliability the task demands, above all for numeric work.

sectionTitle: Choosing Output Formats: Inline, Artifacts, Structured, Code-Executed
question: What is the Inline format for?

options.A: Any output containing numbers that have to be trusted
options.B: Documents and code you intend to refine and reuse
options.C: Data that downstream tools or readers will consume directly
options.D: Conversational responses you will act on within the chat — quick and contextual, not a standalone artifact

explanation: Inline is the quick contextual reply, not a deliverable.

sectionTitle: Choosing Output Formats: Inline, Artifacts, Structured, Code-Executed
question: What are Artifacts for?

options.A: Documents and code — a separate, editable block you will refine and reuse; the right home for a deliverable rather than a reply
options.B: Quick conversational answers you act on immediately
options.C: Tables and defined schemas consumed by downstream tools
options.D: Calculations that must be computed rather than written

explanation: Artifacts hold deliverables you will refine and reuse.

sectionTitle: Choosing Output Formats: Inline, Artifacts, Structured, Code-Executed
question: What are structured formats for?

options.A: Any output that has been escalated for human override
options.B: Conversational replies that stay inside the chat
options.C: Long-form documents a recipient will open and read
options.D: Data — tables and defined schemas that downstream tools or readers can consume directly

explanation: Structured output exists so downstream consumers can use it without restructuring.

sectionTitle: Choosing Output Formats: Inline, Artifacts, Structured, Code-Executed
question: What is the rule for code execution as the verified-output path?

options.A: Prose generation is more reliable for arithmetic because it shows the reasoning in words
options.B: Use code execution for every output regardless of its content
options.C: When numbers must be right, have Claude compute them rather than write them — code execution returns a computed, checkable result along with the steps
options.D: Code execution removes the need for human review of numeric work

explanation: Computed numbers are traceable; generated numbers are plausible-looking guesses.

sectionTitle: Choosing Output Formats: Inline, Artifacts, Structured, Code-Executed
question: What limitation does the lesson attach to code execution?

options.A: Code execution cannot handle files as large as a spreadsheet
options.B: Claude writes the code, so the logic can still contain a bug — the guarantee is that you can read, verify, and re-run the calculation, not that it is automatically correct
options.C: Code execution hides its steps, so the result cannot be audited
options.D: There is no limitation; a computed result is correct by definition

explanation: The guarantee is auditability and reproducibility, not automatic correctness.

sectionTitle: Choosing Output Formats: Inline, Artifacts, Structured, Code-Executed
question: Asked for total Q3 revenue and the top three accounts from an uploaded spreadsheet, the prose path returned 'about $4.7 million' plus three account names. What is wrong with it?

options.A: It listed the accounts in the wrong order, which is the only real error
options.B: It is too short; the same figures in a longer answer would be reliable
options.C: It is fluent, fast, and unverifiable — the total is the model's best guess at summing a column it cannot reliably add, and a wrong total propagates into every downstream decision
options.D: Nothing is wrong; prose figures are acceptable for any reporting purpose

explanation: A prose figure is a number-shaped guess, and the error travels with every decision built on it.

sectionTitle: Choosing Output Formats: Inline, Artifacts, Structured, Code-Executed
question: What does the code-executed path return for that same task?

options.A: Claude writes and runs code over the actual file, returning a computed sum, the top accounts ranked by their real totals, and a chart — traceable to the rows that produced it
options.B: Claude estimates the sum and then formats it as a table for clarity
options.C: Claude retrieves a comparable figure from its training data and cites the source
options.D: Claude asks the user to confirm the total before reporting it

explanation: The computed figure ($4,712,380 in the example) is traceable back to the rows that produced it.

sectionTitle: Choosing Output Formats: Inline, Artifacts, Structured, Code-Executed
question: Is the prose answer simply the lazy option?

options.A: No — prose and code-executed figures are equally reliable in every case
options.B: Yes — prose figures should never be produced under any circumstances
options.C: Yes — prose output indicates the wrong model tier was selected
options.D: No — it is a different kind of output, and for a low-stakes gut-check it may be fine; the reliability requirement is what points to code execution

explanation: Prose is fine for a low-stakes gut-check; anything that gets reported points to code execution.

sectionTitle: Choosing Output Formats: Inline, Artifacts, Structured, Code-Executed
question: What is the selection rule for output modality?

options.A: Pick the output modality by how the recipient prefers to read
options.B: Pick the output modality by the reliability the task requires
options.C: Pick the output modality by the expected length of the answer
options.D: Default to structured formats, which are reliable for every purpose

explanation: Reliability requirement drives the modality choice.

sectionTitle: Choosing Output Formats: Inline, Artifacts, Structured, Code-Executed
question: Which three techniques does the lesson name for curating inputs?

options.A: De-duplicate your sources, label and structure what you supply, and prune material irrelevant to the question
options.B: Upload as much material as possible, compress it, and let Claude select what matters
options.C: Convert every input to a table, sort it, and cite it inline
options.D: Split inputs across several conversations, one document per session

explanation: De-duplicate, label, prune — these three do most of the work.

sectionTitle: Choosing Output Formats: Inline, Artifacts, Structured, Code-Executed
question: Why does curating inputs mean removing material as well as adding it?

options.A: Because uploading more than three documents is not supported
options.B: Because noise in the input becomes noise in the output — clean, well-labeled, minimal inputs produce a cleaner result than a large undifferentiated pile
options.C: Because curation affects processing speed but not output quality
options.D: Because curation is only necessary when code execution is unavailable

explanation: Organized inputs produce organized outputs; the wrong material has to come out, not just the right material go in.

question: Triage exercise, Output A: an internal brainstorm of campaign ideas, clearly labeled as a starting point, with a few generic entries among strong ones. What is the verdict?

options.A: Needs human override — campaign ideas carry reputational risk
options.B: Needs revision — every generic entry must be replaced before the list can be used
options.C: Ready to use — low stakes, internal, and explicitly a starting point; the generic entries do not make it unfit for its purpose
options.D: Ready to use, but only once the ideas have been checked with code execution

explanation: Depth of review follows the stakes; a labeled internal starting point clears the bar as it stands.

question: Triage exercise, Output B: a financial summary stating a total that does not match the sum of the line items above it. What is the verdict?

options.A: Ready to use — the mismatch is a formatting artifact rather than a calculation error
options.B: Ready to use — the line items are present, so a reader can correct the total
options.C: Needs human override — any arithmetic error requires escalation to a person
options.D: Needs revision — the gap is specific and identified, so recompute with code execution and reconcile the total before use

explanation: A named, fixable gap is the 'needs revision' case; note that if the same summary fed a regulated filing, the Diligence thresholds would push it to override.

question: Triage exercise, Output C: a market overview citing three statistics, none of which names a source you can check. What is the verdict?

options.A: Ready to use — the statistics are consistent with the rest of the overview
options.B: Needs revision — unsourced specifics are the fabricated-specific pattern, so re-prompt with grounding and auditable citations or remove the figures
options.C: Needs human override — an output without citations can never be repaired
options.D: Ready to use, provided the figures are labeled as approximate

explanation: Three uncheckable statistics is a specific, repairable gap: ground them or drop them.

question: Triage exercise, Output D: a draft regulatory filing summary, accurate on the points you spot-checked, intended for submission to a regulator. What is the verdict?

options.A: Needs human override — regulatory exposure, a regulator as audience, and an irreversible submission outweigh the fact that spot checks passed
options.B: Ready to use — the points you checked were accurate
options.C: Needs revision — a tone pass for the regulator is the only remaining gap
options.D: Ready to use, because labeling it a draft removes the regulatory obligation

explanation: Three of the four thresholds fire at once, and passing spot checks does not substitute for review of a regulated submission.

question: A report is accurate on every figure you checked, but you suspect a relevant factor was left out entirely. What does a complete Discernment review require?

options.A: Re-running the report on a more capable model
options.B: Nothing further; every figure checked out, so the report is sound
options.C: A separate completeness check against the requirements, looking for missing elements rather than wrong ones
options.D: Asking Claude whether it left anything out and trusting the answer

explanation: Accuracy and completeness fail independently, so a clean accuracy pass does not close the completeness question.
