options.A: The defined gate has collapsed in practice — a review step nobody actually performs is functionally no review at all, regardless of the label still attached to it
options.B: The use case has correctly graduated to fully appropriate based on demonstrated accuracy
options.C: Nothing has changed, since the classification label is unaffected by daily practice
options.D: The load-bearing criterion has shifted from accountability to reversibility

explanation: A gate that exists on paper but is not actually performed is the same failure the module warns about: the classification only holds if the gate is real.

question: Which best summarizes the throughline connecting the five lessons of Module 6?

options.A: Treat governance as a compliance function separate from daily practitioner decisions
options.B: Automate every use case a current model is technically capable of performing, then correct errors as they surface
options.C: Screen use cases against the Delegation criteria, vet Skills like any software before granting them access, classify data by sensitivity before it enters a feature, apply policy as a sustained habit rather than a one-time acknowledgment, and evaluate routine output for bias and fairness as part of ordinary review
options.D: Apply a single fixed risk tier to every use case, Skill, and dataset regardless of context

explanation: Each lesson supplies one part of the same practitioner judgment: screen the use case, vet the tool, classify the data, sustain the policy, and watch for ethical risk in ordinary output.

question: What are the two unproductive things most people do when an output disappoints?

options.A: Give up and conclude 'Claude can't do this,' or thrash by changing random things until something works
options.B: Switch to a higher model tier or restart the conversation immediately
options.C: Escalate to a colleague or lower the task's scope
options.D: Report a bug or request a refund

explanation: The module opens by naming these two unproductive defaults before offering a sequence to replace them.

question: What is context overload, and what does it show up as?

options.B: The prompt left out context, constraints, or the format

options.D: A knowledge source that has drifted out of date

question: Why does diagnosing the four failure patterns require reading the timing and pattern of the symptom, not just the bad output itself?

question: How do wrong-feature-or-model failures show up?

options.A: Check the feature and model: is this a calculation that needs code execution, or a complex task on a speed-tier model?
options.B: Re-read the prompt against the five components: is anything under-specified?
options.C: Check the conversation length: is context overloaded and in need of a restart or summary?
options.D: Check the configuration: are the instructions, knowledge, and Skills current?

question: What is step 3 of the diagnostic sequence?

options.A: Check the configuration: are the instructions, knowledge, and Skills current?
options.B: Re-read the prompt against the five components: is anything under-specified?
options.C: Check the conversation length: is context overloaded and in need of a restart or summary?
options.D: Check the feature and model: is this a calculation that needs code execution, or a complex task on a speed-tier model?

question: What is step 4 of the diagnostic sequence?

options.A: Re-read the prompt against the five components: is anything under-specified?

options.D: Check the feature and model: is this a calculation that needs code execution?

options.D: A repeatable procedure with steps

explanation: Procedures go to Skills, per the quick test.

sectionTitle: Optimizing Workflows for Efficiency and Effectiveness
question: What is the quick test for where a fix belongs?

options.A: Is it reversible, consequential, or accountable? Score it against the Delegation criteria
options.B: Is it a rule, a reference, or a procedure? Rules go to instructions, references go to knowledge, procedures go to Skills
options.C: Is it urgent, routine, or exploratory? Route it by priority
options.D: Is it text, numeric, or visual? Route it by output type

explanation: This three-way test is the lesson's method for choosing the right configuration home.

sectionTitle: Optimizing Workflows for Efficiency and Effectiveness
question: Why does putting a fix in the wrong home cause some 'optimizations' to not stick?

options.A: A procedure pasted as a one-line instruction loses its steps, and reference material crammed into an instruction bloats every prompt
options.B: Because the wrong home always triggers an error message
options.C: Because only Anthropic-provided Skills can hold procedures
options.D: Because standing instructions cannot reference the knowledge base

explanation: Mismatched homes degrade the fix itself, which is why the promotion has to land correctly.

sectionTitle: Optimizing Workflows for Efficiency and Effectiveness
question: What caution does the lesson add about promoting a fix into configuration?

options.A: Promote fixes only after they have been reviewed by an administrator
options.B: Promote every fix immediately, since delay compounds the cost of friction
options.C: Only promote fixes that have been used successfully at least ten times
options.D: Run the workflow a few cycles with the old approach still available before fully relying on the new setup, since not every change is an improvement

explanation: A trial period before full reliance is the lesson's stated caution.

sectionTitle: Optimizing Workflows for Efficiency and Effectiveness
question: Why does the lesson recommend proving the gain on a few runs before committing?

options.A: Because Claude requires several runs before a Skill can be finalized
options.B: The compounding benefit of optimization is real, but so is the compounding cost of a bad change baked into a workflow everyone uses
options.C: Because Projects cannot be edited more than once per day
options.D: Because standing instructions take several sessions to take effect

explanation: Both the benefit and the risk of a shared workflow change compound, which is why the change is proven first.

sectionTitle: Optimizing Workflows for Efficiency and Effectiveness
question: Why is optimization you cannot measure hard to justify or sustain?

options.A: Because there is no concrete gain to track or point to
options.B: Because Claude will not apply an unmeasured optimization
options.C: Because unmeasured optimizations always turn out to be false improvements
options.D: Because measurement is required before a fix can be promoted to a Skill

explanation: Without a tracked gain, there is nothing to point to that justifies keeping the change.

sectionTitle: Optimizing Workflows for Efficiency and Effectiveness
question: What are the concrete gains the lesson says to track?

options.A: Number of standing instructions written and knowledge base size
options.B: Model tier used, number of Skills enabled, and number of conversations held
options.C: Time saved per cycle, revision cycles reduced, and consistency improved across people doing the same task
options.D: Usage-limit consumption and account plan tier

explanation: These three concrete gains are what the lesson recommends tracking.

sectionTitle: Optimizing Workflows for Efficiency and Effectiveness
question: What does identifying the right metric up front also tell you?

options.A: Whether the workflow should be run in a Project or in Chat
options.B: Which model tier the workflow should use
options.C: When to stop — optimization has diminishing returns, and once the metric you care about is good enough, further tuning is its own kind of friction
options.D: How many people should be granted access to the workflow

explanation: Knowing the target metric is also what tells you when further optimization stops paying off.

sectionTitle: Optimizing Workflows for Efficiency and Effectiveness
question: In the worked example, what were the three frictions the audit found in the weekly reporting workflow?

options.A: Each analyst uploads a different dataset, each uses a different format, and each writes different standing instructions
options.B: Each analyst uses a different model tier, each works in a separate Project, and each skips the review step
options.C: Each analyst re-types the same calculation, each uses a different entry point, and each has different Skill access
options.D: Each analyst re-pastes the same background, each reformats the output by hand, and each catches different things

explanation: These three frictions were what the audit surfaced in the 45-minute workflow.

sectionTitle: Optimizing Workflows for Efficiency and Effectiveness
question: In that same worked example, what was the optimization applied to each friction?

options.A: The background moved into a shared Project knowledge base, a Skill was added for the report format, and a standing instruction was set for the verification step
options.B: The background moved into a Skill, the report format moved into the knowledge base, and the verification step moved into Memory
options.C: All three frictions were resolved by upgrading the model tier used by the team
options.D: All three frictions were resolved by consolidating the team into a single conversation

explanation: This maps each friction to its correct configuration home, matching the rule-reference-procedure test.

sectionTitle: Optimizing Workflows for Efficiency and Effectiveness
question: What was the measured result of that optimization?

options.A: About 25 minutes per analyst, but format still varied by who ran it
options.B: About 25 minutes per analyst, consistent format across the team, and one fewer revision round
options.C: The same 45 minutes per analyst, but with fewer revision rounds
options.D: About 15 minutes per analyst, with no change in consistency

explanation: Time, consistency, and revision rounds all improved together in the worked example.

sectionTitle: Optimizing Workflows for Efficiency and Effectiveness
question: How does the worked example map onto the rule-reference-procedure test?

options.A: The repeated background (a reference) went to the knowledge base, the report format (a procedure) went to a Skill, and the verification step (a rule) went to a standing instruction
options.B: The repeated background (a rule) went to a standing instruction, the report format (a reference) went to the knowledge base, and the verification step (a procedure) went to a Skill
options.C: All three frictions were treated as procedures and went to Skills
options.D: All three frictions were treated as rules and went to standing instructions

explanation: Each friction was sorted correctly by type: reference, procedure, and rule, into their matching homes.

question: Quiz: You open a brand-new chat and ask Claude to draft a vendor renewal email. Its very first response is generic and ignores the two contract terms you most need to flag. Nothing degraded over time; the opening answer was already off. What is the most likely root cause?

options.A: Stale configuration; a standing instruction has drifted out of date
options.B: Context overload; the conversation neared its limit and early instructions were summarized away
options.C: Under-specification; the prompt never named the contract terms or context that mattered, so the first answer was already off
options.D: Wrong feature; the task needed code execution

explanation: First-response-wrong, in a brand-new chat, is the signature of under-specification, not the other three patterns.

question: Quiz: You ask Claude for a thorough competitive analysis, but every response stays shallow and skims the surface even after you add detail. You had selected a fast, lightweight model tier to save time. Which diagnosis fits, and what is the fix?

options.A: Stale configuration; the analysis depends on a knowledge source that has drifted
options.B: Under-specification; keep adding more context until the depth improves
options.C: Context overload; restart the session from a summary
options.D: Wrong model tier; switch to a more capable model built for deep analysis rather than a speed-tier model

explanation: Adding detail did not help, which rules out under-specification; a speed-tier model on a depth task is the named wrong-feature-or-model case.

question: Quiz: An output disappoints. What should you do before concluding Claude cannot do the task?

options.A: Immediately switch to the most capable model
options.B: Run the diagnostic sequence: check specification, context length, feature/model, then configuration
options.C: Rewrite the prompt from scratch repeatedly until it works
options.D: Abandon the task and do it manually

explanation: The full ordered sequence runs before any conclusion that the task itself is unfit.

question: Quiz: A recurring report needs the same manual correction every week. What is the most durable fix?

options.A: Keep making the correction by hand each week
options.B: Capture the fix as a standing instruction or Skill in the Project so it persists
options.C: Switch models each week
options.D: Start a fresh conversation each time and re-explain

explanation: Only capturing the fix into configuration removes the recurring manual cost.

question: Quiz: A team's monthly close report takes about six hours and the numbers are reliable, but three analysts each format their section differently, so a reviewer spends about 90 minutes reconciling styles before sign-off. The goal is to cut that 90-minute reconciliation time. Which optimization delivers the biggest measured gain against that metric?

options.A: Add a second reviewer to split the reconciliation work.
options.B: Upgrade the model tier the analysts use so each section is drafted faster.
options.C: Ask the analysts to start their sections earlier in the month.
options.D: Create one shared Skill that formats every section to a single template, so all three sections arrive in the same style.

explanation: The bottleneck is inconsistent formatting, not drafting speed or reviewer capacity, so a shared formatting Skill targets the actual metric.

question: According to Key Takeaway 1, what should happen before blaming the tool?

options.A: Run the diagnostic sequence — specification, context, feature, configuration
options.B: Switch to a more capable model tier
options.C: Escalate the task to a human reviewer
options.D: Rewrite the prompt from scratch

explanation: Takeaway 1: underperformance has discoverable causes.

question: According to Key Takeaway 2, what does isolating the failure require?

options.A: Naming which entry point was used
options.B: Naming which model tier produced the output
options.C: Naming whether the failure is the prompt, the context, the feature choice, or an expectation mismatch
options.D: Naming which Delegation criterion applies

explanation: Takeaway 2: isolate before you fix.

question: According to Key Takeaway 3, what should happen with a disappointing output?

options.A: Escalate it to a colleague for a second opinion
options.B: Discard it and start over with a completely different prompt
options.C: Translate the critique into a specific adjustment, then capture the fix as an instruction or Skill so it persists
options.D: Log it and move on without further action

explanation: Takeaway 3: every disappointing output is data.

question: According to Key Takeaway 4, what does optimizing deliberately require?

options.A: Upgrade the model tier used across the whole workflow
options.B: Instrument the workflow, find the friction, promote the fix into configuration, and measure the gain
options.C: Consolidate every workflow into a single shared Project
options.D: Escalate every recurring workflow to Developer expertise

explanation: Takeaway 4: optimize deliberately.

question: Per the module's disclaimer, how should the course's examples and scenarios be treated?

options.A: As unnecessary to verify against current documentation
options.B: As guaranteed accurate and unlikely to change
options.C: As legally binding professional guidance
options.D: As illustrative and often fictitious; mentioning a company or product does not imply endorsement in either direction

explanation: The disclaimer explicitly frames examples as illustrative and non-endorsing, matching earlier modules.

question: What does the module's sources note list as cross-references to earlier modules?

options.A: Context management (Module 1), diagnostic iteration (Module 2), configuration maintenance (Module 5)
options.B: Prompt anatomy (Module 2), entry points (Module 1), Delegation mapping (Module 4)
options.C: Skill trust (Module 6), data sensitivity (Module 6), organizational policy (Module 6)
options.D: Requirements analysis (Module 4), research synthesis (Module 4), solution design (Module 4)

explanation: These three specific cross-references are named in the sources section.

question: A team notices Claude's output has been degrading gradually over the course of a long single session, though the same setup worked fine at the start of the conversation. Applying this module's timing-pattern logic, which diagnosis fits best?

options.A: Context overload — it started fine and degraded as the conversation grew
options.B: Under-specification — the prompt never carried what it needed from the start
options.C: Wrong feature or model — a calculation is being generated instead of computed
options.D: Stale configuration — a Skill or knowledge source has drifted out of date

explanation: Fine-at-the-start, degraded-over-time is the timing signature the module attaches specifically to context overload.

question: A team wants both a fixable output problem addressed and the fix made durable for future use. Applying this module's throughline, what does that require in sequence?

options.A: Rewrite the prompt from scratch, then repeat that rewrite at the start of every future session
options.B: Escalate the problem to a higher model tier, then document the escalation for future reference
options.C: Restart the conversation from a summary, then rely on Memory to retain the correction
options.D: Diagnose the failure with the sequence to find the specific fix, then capture that fix as a standing instruction or Skill so it does not have to be rediscovered

explanation: Diagnosis finds the fix; capture is what makes the fix durable — the two lessons work in sequence.

question: Which best summarizes the throughline connecting the three lessons of Module 7?

options.A: Treat every disappointing output as an expectation mismatch and reshape the task rather than adjusting the prompt
options.B: Always switch to a more capable model whenever an output disappoints, since capability is the most common root cause
options.C: Diagnose underperformance with a disciplined, cheapest-first sequence, translate what the output reveals into a specific, capturable adjustment, and then optimize the whole workflow by finding friction and promoting fixes into the right configuration home
options.D: Optimize workflows first, then diagnose individual outputs only if the optimization does not resolve them

explanation: Each lesson supplies one stage of the same practice: diagnose the specific failure, translate and capture the fix, then optimize the workflow it belongs to.

sectionTitle: Choosing the Right Entry Point, Model & Features
question: A marketing associate needs quick, one-off drafts of email subject lines for tomorrow's campaign. No integration with any other tool is needed. Which entry point best fits the task?

options.A: The Claude.ai chat interface
options.B: A custom build on the API
options.C: Claude Code
options.D: An MCP server connected to the CRM

explanation: For a single, low-volume, non-recurring task with no integration need, the standalone chat interface is the fastest and lowest-overhead option; building an API integration for a one-off task adds unnecessary engineering overhead.

sectionTitle: Choosing the Right Entry Point, Model & Features
question: A support team wants Claude's replies to appear automatically inside their existing ticketing system, with no agent ever opening a separate chat window. What does this requirement point to?

options.A: A Projects workspace in the chat interface
options.B: API-based integration into the ticketing system
options.C: Asking agents to copy-paste from Claude.ai
options.D: A one-time custom instruction change

explanation: Embedding Claude's output directly into another application's interface, invisibly to the end user, is a defining signal for an API integration rather than the standalone chat product.

sectionTitle: Choosing the Right Entry Point, Model & Features
question: A team runs a very high-volume, low-complexity classification task (tagging thousands of short support tickets by category) and is sensitive to cost and latency. What should guide model selection?

options.A: Always default to the most capable model available, regardless of task
options.B: Match the model tier to task complexity — a faster, lower-cost model for simple, high-volume classification
options.C: Model choice never affects cost or speed
options.D: Use the largest context window model regardless of the task

explanation: Matching model capability to task complexity is a core competency: high-volume, low-complexity tasks are usually better served by a faster, cheaper model tier, reserving the most capable tier for tasks that need deeper reasoning.

sectionTitle: Choosing the Right Entry Point, Model & Features
question: A policy team needs Claude to consistently reference the same 40-page internal compliance handbook across dozens of conversations, without re-uploading it each time. Which feature addresses this most directly?

options.A: A persistent knowledge base attached to a Project
options.B: A single very long chat message
options.C: Switching models each time
options.D: Disabling custom instructions

explanation: Persistent, reusable knowledge attached to a project-style workspace is designed exactly for recurring reference material, avoiding repeated uploads and keeping answers grounded in the same source.

sectionTitle: Choosing the Right Entry Point, Model & Features
question: A sales rep wants every outbound email to automatically pull the recipient's latest CRM activity before Claude drafts the message, with no manual copying. What entry point is required?

options.A: The standalone chat interface only
options.B: An integration that connects Claude to the CRM programmatically
options.C: A downloaded PDF export of the CRM
options.D: A shared spreadsheet of past emails

explanation: Automatically pulling live data from another system into a Claude-generated draft requires a programmatic integration, not a manual chat workflow.

sectionTitle: Choosing the Right Entry Point, Model & Features
question: A task requires Claude to look something up, decide the next step based on the result, and then take a second action — repeating this loop until a goal is met. What best describes the right shape for this task?

options.A: A single-shot prompt with no follow-up
options.B: A multi-step, tool-using agentic workflow
options.C: A static FAQ document
options.D: A one-time chat message with no context

explanation: Tasks that require iterative lookup-decide-act loops are the signature use case for an agentic, multi-step workflow rather than a single-shot prompt.

sectionTitle: Choosing the Right Entry Point, Model & Features
question: A company is moving from a handful of individual employees experimenting with Claude to a company-wide rollout that needs SSO, usage oversight, and admin controls. What does this shift require?

options.A: Nothing — individual accounts scale to any size automatically
options.B: A governed, organization-level deployment with admin and access controls
options.C: Asking every employee to share one login
options.D: Switching entirely to Claude Code

explanation: Moving from individual experimentation to organization-wide use is the signal to move to a governed deployment with centralized administration, access control, and oversight — not ad hoc individual accounts.

question: A prompt needs to give Claude background context, a set of instructions, and two worked examples, all clearly separated so nothing is confused with anything else. What technique best supports this?

options.A: Writing everything as one unbroken paragraph
options.B: Using clear separators (such as labeled sections or tags) to distinguish context, instructions, and examples
options.C: Repeating the instructions three times in a row
options.D: Removing the examples to keep the prompt short

explanation: Clearly separating distinct parts of a prompt — context, instructions, examples — reduces ambiguity and is a foundational structured-prompting technique.

question: A workflow requires Claude's output to always be valid, strictly-formatted JSON that a downstream script can parse without errors. What's the most reliable way to get this consistently?

options.A: Hope the model infers the right format
options.B: Explicitly specify the required format and show a concrete example of correct output
options.C: Ask for JSON once and never check again
options.D: Switch to a shorter prompt with fewer details

explanation: Explicit format instructions paired with a concrete example are the most reliable way to get consistent, machine-parseable output.

question: A task has several tricky edge cases that keep getting handled inconsistently. What's the best first fix?

options.A: Add few-shot examples that specifically cover those edge cases
options.B: Shorten the prompt so it's less confusing
options.C: Switch to a completely different task
options.D: Remove all instructions and let the model decide

explanation: Targeted examples that demonstrate how to handle known edge cases are one of the most effective ways to reduce inconsistent handling of tricky inputs.

question: A task involves multi-step reasoning over conflicting figures in a financial summary before reaching a conclusion. Which prompting approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Asking for the final answer only, with no reasoning shown
options.B: Encouraging step-by-step reasoning before the final answer
options.C: Using a single-word response format
options.D: Avoiding any explanation of the task's goal

explanation: Encouraging step-by-step reasoning is most appropriate for tasks that involve working through multiple, possibly conflicting pieces of information before concluding.

question: A team wants every customer-facing reply to share the same tone and role across many different agents and conversations. What should be set up?

options.A: A consistent role/persona and tone defined in the system or custom instructions
options.B: Nothing — tone will naturally stay consistent on its own
options.C: A new prompt written from scratch by each agent every time
options.D: Disabling instructions entirely

explanation: Defining a consistent role, tone, and persona once in shared instructions is how consistency is maintained across many users and conversations.

question: The first version of a prompt produces answers that are accurate but wildly inconsistent in formatting from one run to the next. What should be adjusted first?

options.A: Switch to a completely different, more expensive model
options.B: Tighten the output-format instructions and add an example of the desired format
options.C: Abandon the task as not feasible
options.D: Remove all context from the prompt

explanation: When accuracy is fine but formatting is inconsistent, the issue is almost always the prompt's format guidance — tightening instructions and adding an example usually resolves it before a model change is warranted.

question: A prompt that worked well for a creative brainstorming task is reused unchanged for a strict data-extraction task, and the output becomes unreliable. What's the best explanation and fix?

options.A: Creative and extraction tasks need the same open-ended structure — no change needed
options.B: The prompt structure should be adapted to the task type — extraction needs tighter constraints and a defined schema, not open-ended framing
options.C: The model is incapable of ever doing extraction tasks
options.D: Extraction tasks should never use any structure at all

explanation: Prompt structure should match the nature of the task: open-ended framing suits creative work, while extraction tasks need tighter constraints, such as a defined schema, to be reliable.

question: A complex task keeps failing when handled as one giant instruction. What restructuring is most likely to help?

options.A: Breaking the task into smaller, sequential subtasks with clear handoffs
options.B: Making the single instruction even longer and more detailed
options.C: Removing all structure and letting the model guess the steps
options.D: Repeating the same instruction multiple times in the prompt

explanation: Breaking a complex task with many dependent steps into smaller, well-defined subtasks with clear handoffs generally improves reliability over one large, monolithic instruction.

sectionTitle: Validating Output & Knowing When Human Review Is Mandatory
question: Claude drafts a clause for a legal contract that will be sent to an external partner. What is the appropriate next step before it goes out?

options.A: Send it immediately since Claude drafted it
options.B: Mandatory human (ideally legal) review before it is used externally
options.C: Skip review because the language sounds professional
options.D: Ask Claude to confirm it is correct and treat that as sufficient

explanation: High-stakes, externally-binding content such as legal language requires mandatory qualified human review before use — the model's own self-assessment is not a substitute for that review.

sectionTitle: Validating Output & Knowing When Human Review Is Mandatory
question: An employee asks Claude to summarize their own internal meeting notes purely for personal reference, with no distribution to anyone else. What level of review is appropriate?

options.A: Full legal review before reading it
options.B: A light personal spot-check is reasonable given the low stakes and internal-only use
options.C: No review is ever appropriate for any Claude output
options.D: Escalation to a compliance team is required

explanation: Review intensity should scale with stakes and audience; a low-stakes, personal-use summary reasonably needs only a light spot-check, not a formal review process.

sectionTitle: Validating Output & Knowing When Human Review Is Mandatory
question: Before publishing a customer-facing article that Claude drafted using several source documents, what should be verified?

options.A: That the draft sounds fluent and confident
options.B: That specific factual claims and figures are grounded in and consistent with the source documents
options.C: Nothing further, since Claude cited its sources
options.D: Only the grammar and spelling

explanation: Fluency is not evidence of accuracy; grounding specific claims and figures back to the actual source material is the necessary check before publication.

sectionTitle: Validating Output & Knowing When Human Review Is Mandatory
question: A report Claude produced includes a specific statistic attributed to an external study. What should a careful reviewer do?

options.A: Trust the figure because it appears in the output
options.B: Verify the statistic against the original source before relying on it
options.C: Remove all numbers from every report going forward
options.D: Assume Claude never makes factual errors

explanation: Specific factual claims, especially numeric ones, should be verified against original sources rather than trusted solely because they appear confidently in the output.

sectionTitle: Validating Output & Knowing When Human Review Is Mandatory
question: A company wants to use Claude to help make automated decisions about individual loan applications. What review structure does this call for?

options.A: Full automation with no human involvement, since it's more efficient
options.B: A human-in-the-loop review for decisions that materially affect individuals
options.C: Random spot-checks once a year
options.D: No review, since the model is described as accurate

explanation: Decisions with material, individual-level consequences (like loan approvals) call for human-in-the-loop review, not full automation, regardless of general model accuracy.

sectionTitle: Validating Output & Knowing When Human Review Is Mandatory
question: Which situation is the strongest signal to be extra cautious about possible hallucination in Claude's output?

options.A: A request to reformat a document the user provided
options.B: A request for a very recent, narrow, or obscure fact that isn't in any provided source
options.C: A request to summarize a short paragraph that was pasted into the chat
options.D: A request to rephrase a sentence for clarity

explanation: Requests for very recent, narrow, or obscure facts not grounded in provided source material carry the highest risk of confidently incorrect (hallucinated) output, warranting extra verification.

sectionTitle: Validating Output & Knowing When Human Review Is Mandatory
question: A team runs a high-volume pipeline where Claude classifies thousands of records per day. Full manual review of every output isn't feasible. What's a reasonable validation approach?

options.A: Skip all validation since volume is too high
options.B: Set up periodic sampling/spot-checks with defined quality thresholds
options.C: Only check outputs if a customer complains
options.D: Validate once at launch and never again

explanation: For high-volume automated pipelines, structured sampling with defined quality thresholds is the practical way to maintain ongoing confidence in output quality without reviewing every single item.

sectionTitle: Validating Output & Knowing When Human Review Is Mandatory
question: A user disagrees with how Claude characterized an ambiguous data trend in a report. What is the best next step?

options.A: Treat Claude's characterization as final and non-negotiable
options.B: Go back to the underlying data and treat Claude's output as an advisory starting point, not the final authority
options.C: Discard the data entirely
options.D: Assume the user is simply wrong

explanation: On ambiguous judgment calls, Claude's output should be treated as an advisory draft to check against the underlying data — not as an unquestionable final authority.

question: A weekly status report is currently drafted entirely by hand from the same recurring data sources. Which change reflects sound delegation practice?

options.A: Leave the entire process manual indefinitely
options.B: Have Claude draft the routine first pass from the data, with a human reviewing and finalizing it
options.C: Fully automate the report with no human review at any point
options.D: Delegate the task but stop checking it after the first success

explanation: Routine, recurring drafting work is a strong candidate for delegation to Claude, paired with a human review-and-finalize checkpoint rather than either full manual work or fully unchecked automation.

question: In a multi-step agent workflow that ends with sending an email to an external client, where is the most important checkpoint to place?

options.A: At the very beginning, before any drafting starts
options.B: Immediately before the irreversible, external-facing action (sending the email)
options.C: There is no need for any checkpoint
options.D: Only after the email has already been sent

explanation: Checkpoints are most valuable right before irreversible, external-facing actions, since that is the last point where a human can catch and correct a problem before it has real-world consequences.

question: A team wants to fully automate a final client-facing legal opinion with no human review at any stage, to save time. What's the concern with this plan?

options.A: There is no concern — automation is always safe when it saves time
options.B: This is over-delegation of a high-stakes, externally-binding task that should retain human review
options.C: Legal work is too simple to need review
options.D: Automation should only ever be used for low-value tasks

explanation: Fully removing human review from a high-stakes, externally-binding output like a legal opinion is over-delegation; the consequences of an error are too significant to skip review.

question: An employee spends hours every week manually reformatting the same type of routine document into a standard template, a task with low ambiguity and low risk. What does this represent?

options.A: Appropriate use of human time
options.B: A likely case of under-delegation — a good candidate to hand to Claude with review
options.C: A task that should never be automated under any circumstances
options.D: A task that requires Architect-level system design

explanation: Low-ambiguity, low-risk, repetitive tasks like standard reformatting are classic under-delegation cases — well suited to being handed to Claude with a lightweight review step.

question: When mapping a workflow before deciding what to delegate, what should be identified for each step?

options.A: Only the final output, ignoring how it's produced
options.B: The inputs, the decision points, and the outputs of each step
options.C: Nothing — workflow mapping is unnecessary before delegating
options.D: Only which employee currently does the task

explanation: Mapping the inputs, decision points, and outputs of each step is what allows a clear-eyed assessment of which parts of a workflow are safe and useful to delegate.

question: A customer-service escalation workflow needs clear rules for when a case is handed from Claude-assisted drafting to a human agent. Which of these should trigger escalation?

options.A: Every single case, regardless of content
options.B: A novel policy question, a financial threshold being exceeded, or a highly sensitive complaint
options.C: Only cases where the customer says 'thank you'
options.D: No cases should ever escalate once the workflow is set up

explanation: Well-designed escalation criteria target situations with elevated risk or novelty — novel policy questions, financial thresholds, and sensitive complaints — rather than escalating everything or nothing.

question: An agent is being configured to handle both scheduling meetings and sending external client communications. How should its autonomy be set?

options.A: Grant the same high level of autonomy to both actions
options.B: Match autonomy to the reversibility and risk of each action — more oversight for the harder-to-reverse, external action
options.C: Give it no autonomy at all for either action
options.D: Autonomy level should be random

explanation: Autonomy should scale with how reversible and risky an action is; a low-risk, reversible action (scheduling) can carry more autonomy than a higher-risk, harder-to-reverse action (external client communication).

question: A workflow map shows that a Claude-assisted step routinely produces incorrect output whenever a particular input type appears. What does this suggest for delegation design?

options.A: Nothing needs to change
options.B: That step needs a redesigned checkpoint or added guardrail specifically for that input type, not blanket removal of Claude from the workflow
options.C: The entire workflow should be abandoned
options.D: The issue should be ignored until a customer complains

explanation: A recurring failure tied to a specific input type calls for a targeted fix — a checkpoint or guardrail for that case — rather than either ignoring it or discarding the whole workflow.

question: A specific formatting preference comes up in almost every conversation a team has with Claude. What's the better long-term fix versus repeating it each time?

options.A: Keep retyping the preference in every single chat
options.B: Add it once to the project's or team's custom instructions
options.C: Ask each employee to memorize it instead
options.D: Ignore the preference since it's minor

explanation: A recurring, stable preference belongs in persistent custom instructions so it applies automatically going forward, instead of being retyped in every conversation.

question: A project's knowledge base still contains last year's pricing sheet, which has since changed. What risk does this create, and what should be done?

options.A: No risk — older documents never affect answers
options.B: Outdated documents can be cited as if current; stale material should be removed or replaced with the current version
options.C: The whole project should be deleted
options.D: Nothing, since Claude always prioritizes the newest fact automatically regardless of what's uploaded

explanation: Stale reference material can be surfaced and cited as though it were current, so keeping a knowledge base curated and up to date is part of ongoing environment maintenance.

question: A project's knowledge base has grown to include many documents that are only loosely related to its actual purpose. What's the likely effect?

options.A: It always improves answer quality to add more documents, regardless of relevance
options.B: It can dilute relevance and increase the chance of citing the wrong document
options.C: It has no effect on output quality
options.D: It automatically reorganizes itself for relevance

explanation: Including loosely related or irrelevant documents in a knowledge base can dilute retrieval relevance and increase the risk of drawing on the wrong source.

question: When setting up a shared team environment, what should be considered regarding who can see or edit what?

options.A: Give every team member identical, unrestricted access by default
options.B: Define access and permissions appropriate to each person's role
options.C: Permissions don't matter for internal tools
options.D: Only the most senior person should ever have any access

explanation: Configuring role-appropriate access and permissions is a basic part of setting up a governed, shared environment, rather than defaulting to unrestricted access for everyone.

question: A new employee joins a team that has been using a Claude project for months. What's the best way to bring them up to speed on how it should be used?

options.A: Expect them to infer the conventions by trial and error
options.B: Point them to clearly documented project instructions and conventions
options.C: Give them a completely separate, undocumented setup
options.D: Tell them documentation isn't necessary since the tool is intuitive

explanation: Clear, written documentation of a project's instructions and conventions is what allows new team members to use a shared environment consistently, rather than relying on undocumented tribal knowledge.

question: A company changes its refund policy. A Claude project used by the support team still has the old policy embedded in its instructions. What should happen?

options.A: Nothing — the instructions will update themselves
options.B: The project's instructions and knowledge should be updated to reflect the new policy
options.C: The project should be left as-is until someone notices an error
options.D: Only verbally tell the team, without updating the project

explanation: When an underlying business process or policy changes, the project's instructions and knowledge need to be actively updated to stay accurate — they don't update automatically.

question: A set of instructions is written so rigidly that it breaks down the moment an unusual case appears, while a looser version causes inconsistent handling of routine cases. What does this illustrate?

options.A: Instructions can never be improved
options.B: The need to balance specificity with flexibility when writing instructions
options.C: That specificity is always bad
options.D: That flexibility is always bad

explanation: Good instruction design balances enough specificity for consistency on routine cases with enough flexibility to handle reasonable variation, rather than erring entirely to one extreme.

sectionTitle: Applying User, Data, Policy & Ethics Guardrails
question: A user wants to paste a document containing customer names, emails, and account numbers into a workflow for summarization. What principle should guide handling this data?

options.A: Include as much data as possible regardless of necessity
options.B: Data minimization — include only the fields actually needed for the task
options.C: Personal data doesn't need any special handling
options.D: Always remove all data and refuse the task

explanation: Data-minimization is a core guardrail: only include the personal data fields genuinely required for the task, reducing unnecessary exposure of sensitive information.

sectionTitle: Applying User, Data, Policy & Ethics Guardrails
question: A colleague is about to type a live production password into a chat prompt so Claude can 'double check' it. What's the appropriate response?

options.A: Encourage it, since Claude can read anything
options.B: Stop them — credentials and secrets should never be entered into a prompt
options.C: Only stop them if the password is longer than 8 characters
options.D: It's fine as long as no one else is in the room

explanation: Credentials and secrets should never be pasted into a prompt; this is a basic data-handling guardrail regardless of the specific tool being used.

sectionTitle: Applying User, Data, Policy & Ethics Guardrails
question: A team wants Claude's customer-facing output to consistently reflect the company's brand voice and ethical commitments. Where should this be codified?

options.A: Nowhere — it should be left to chance each time
options.B: In the project's or system's instructions, so it applies consistently
options.C: Only in a slide deck that nobody references during actual work
options.D: In a document that is never linked to the actual workflow

explanation: Brand and ethical guidelines that need to hold consistently across many interactions should be codified directly in the instructions that govern the workflow, not left as an unreferenced side document.

sectionTitle: Applying User, Data, Policy & Ethics Guardrails
question: A user's prompt asks Claude to do something that conflicts with a documented company policy. Whose guardrail should prevail?

options.A: The individual user's request, always
options.B: The documented company policy
options.C: Whichever is shorter
options.D: Neither — the task should be done exactly halfway

explanation: Governance guardrails exist precisely to hold even when an individual user's request conflicts with them; documented policy should prevail over an individual, ad hoc request.

sectionTitle: Applying User, Data, Policy & Ethics Guardrails
question: A regulated organization is choosing how to deploy Claude for a workflow involving sensitive customer data. What should factor into that decision?

options.A: Nothing beyond convenience
options.B: Data residency, compliance requirements, and applicable regulations for that industry
options.C: Only the visual design of the interface
options.D: The number of employees who like the tool

explanation: For regulated industries handling sensitive data, compliance factors such as data residency and applicable regulations are essential inputs into a deployment decision, not an afterthought.

sectionTitle: Applying User, Data, Policy & Ethics Guardrails
question: A draft created for an internal audience accidentally gets routed toward an external-facing channel, and it contains internal-only figures. What should have caught this?

options.A: Nothing could have caught this
options.B: A review step before external-facing content is sent, checking for inadvertent exposure of internal-only information
options.C: Removing all review steps to move faster
options.D: Assuming internal and external drafts never mix

explanation: A review checkpoint before anything goes external is exactly the safeguard designed to catch accidental exposure of internal-only information before it reaches an outside audience.

sectionTitle: Applying User, Data, Policy & Ethics Guardrails
question: In a regulated workflow, why does it matter to keep a record of which decisions were Claude-assisted and how they were reviewed?

options.A: It doesn't matter and creates unnecessary work
options.B: Auditability supports accountability and compliance if a decision is later questioned
options.C: Only the final output matters, never the process
options.D: Records should be deleted immediately after each decision

explanation: Maintaining an audit trail of Claude-assisted decisions and their review supports accountability and gives the organization a defensible record if a decision is later questioned.

sectionTitle: Applying User, Data, Policy & Ethics Guardrails
question: A screening workflow uses Claude to help shortlist candidates from resumes. What's an appropriate way to manage bias risk in this process?

options.A: Assume there's no bias risk since the model isn't human
options.B: Combine the tool with diverse human review and clear, transparent criteria
options.C: Use the tool with zero human involvement to remove bias entirely
options.D: Ignore the concern since it's not a technical problem

explanation: Managing bias risk in a screening context calls for transparent criteria and diverse human review alongside the tool, rather than assuming automation alone eliminates bias or removing human oversight entirely.

question: Outputs for very similar inputs are coming back inconsistently. What's the best first diagnostic step?

options.A: Immediately conclude the model is incapable of the task
options.B: Check whether the prompt's instructions and examples are specific enough before concluding it's a model limitation
options.C: Abandon the workflow entirely
options.D: Add unrelated instructions to see if something helps

explanation: Inconsistent output is most often a specificity/examples issue in the prompt itself; that should be checked and addressed before assuming the task is beyond the model's capability.

question: A workflow has slowed down because Claude keeps asking clarifying questions before it can proceed. What's the most likely root cause?

options.A: The model is simply too slow in general
options.B: The initial prompt is missing context or is ambiguous about what's being asked
options.C: Clarifying questions are always a sign of a broken workflow with no fix
options.D: This only happens randomly and can't be diagnosed

explanation: Repeated clarifying questions usually point to missing context or ambiguity in the initial prompt — tightening the prompt's context typically resolves it.

question: A team wants to track the ongoing quality of a summarization pipeline over time, not just how fast it runs. What should they measure?

options.A: Speed only
options.B: Periodic accuracy/groundedness spot-checks against source material, in addition to speed
options.C: Nothing — once it works once, it will always work
options.D: The total number of words produced

explanation: Speed alone doesn't capture quality; periodic groundedness or accuracy checks against source material are needed to monitor whether a pipeline's output quality holds up over time.

question: After a knowledge base grows very large, a well-performing workflow starts giving vague or conflicting answers. What's a likely cause and fix?

options.A: The model has permanently lost capability and cannot be fixed
options.B: Irrelevant or conflicting documents are diluting retrieval; pruning the knowledge base to essential, current material can help
options.C: This always means the entire workflow must be abandoned
options.D: Nothing can be done about knowledge base size

explanation: A bloated knowledge base with irrelevant or conflicting material commonly degrades retrieval quality; curating it back down to essential, current documents is a standard fix.

question: A task keeps failing no matter how the prompt is rewritten, because it fundamentally requires real-time data the model has no access to. What does this indicate?

options.A: The prompt just needs one more rewrite and it will work
options.B: This is a task-fit issue, not a prompting issue — the task needs a different tool or integration (such as live data access)
options.C: The team should keep trying indefinitely with prompt changes alone
options.D: This means Claude can never be used for any related task

explanation: When failure is caused by a fundamental capability gap (like lacking real-time data access) rather than prompt wording, that's a task-fit issue requiring a different tool or integration — not more prompt iteration.

question: When testing a revised prompt before rolling it out, what's the best practice?

options.A: Test it once against a single favorable example and ship it
options.B: Test it against a representative sample of varied, realistic inputs, including edge cases
options.C: Skip testing since the previous version worked
options.D: Only test with the easiest possible input

explanation: Testing against a representative, varied sample — including edge cases — gives a much more reliable picture of real-world performance than a single favorable example.

question: A particular step in a workflow has failed the same structural way multiple times despite several prompt tweaks. What does this pattern suggest?

options.A: Another prompt tweak is guaranteed to fix it eventually
options.B: The step or workflow itself may need to be redesigned, not just the prompt patched again
options.C: The team should ignore the recurring failure
options.D: This means the whole product should be abandoned

explanation: A recurring, structural failure that survives multiple prompt tweaks is a signal to redesign the workflow step itself rather than continuing to make small prompt patches.

sectionTitle: The AI Fluency 4Ds & Knowing Your Boundary
question: A user is deciding which parts of a task to hand to Claude and which to keep human-led, based on the task's risk and the model's fit for it. Which AI Fluency competency does this best represent?

options.A: Description
options.B: Delegation
options.C: Discernment
options.D: Diligence

explanation: Delegation is about deciding what to hand off to the AI versus keep human-led, matching the task to an appropriate level of autonomy.

sectionTitle: The AI Fluency 4Ds & Knowing Your Boundary
question: A user carefully spells out the goal, relevant context, constraints, and desired format before asking Claude to do a task. Which competency does this reflect?

options.A: Description
options.B: Delegation
options.C: Discernment
options.D: Diligence

explanation: Description is the competency of clearly articulating context, goals, and constraints so the model has what it needs to perform well.

sectionTitle: The AI Fluency 4Ds & Knowing Your Boundary
question: A user reviews Claude's draft critically, checking its reasoning and claims rather than accepting it at face value. Which competency is this?

options.A: Description
options.B: Delegation
options.C: Discernment
options.D: Diligence

explanation: Discernment is the practice of critically evaluating AI output rather than accepting it uncritically.

sectionTitle: The AI Fluency 4Ds & Knowing Your Boundary
question: A user maintains ongoing oversight of an AI-assisted workflow after it's deployed, rather than deploying it once and never checking on it again. Which competency does this reflect?

options.A: Description
options.B: Delegation
options.C: Discernment
options.D: Diligence

explanation: Diligence is about taking ongoing responsibility for outcomes and maintaining oversight over time, not a 'set it and forget it' approach.

sectionTitle: The AI Fluency 4Ds & Knowing Your Boundary
question: A business user with no engineering background wants to build a custom API integration and multi-agent tool-calling system from scratch. What does sound judgment about scope suggest?

options.A: Attempt the full technical build personally regardless of background
options.B: Recognize this falls outside Associate-level scope and involves the engineering-focused Developer track instead
options.C: There is no meaningful difference between business and engineering tasks
options.D: Avoid using Claude at all if this situation comes up

explanation: Knowing your boundary means recognizing when a task — like building custom integrations and agentic systems — belongs to a more technical role or track, rather than attempting it outside your scope.

sectionTitle: The AI Fluency 4Ds & Knowing Your Boundary
question: A business user is asked to design the enterprise-wide security architecture and governance model for a company's entire Claude deployment. What does this scope call for?

options.A: This is squarely Associate-level work and should be handled solo
options.B: This is Architect-level system design work, which goes beyond the Associate scope
options.C: It should be assigned to whichever employee is available, regardless of role
options.D: It requires no special expertise at all

explanation: End-to-end system design, security architecture, and governance at the enterprise level is Architect-level scope — well beyond what an Associate-level role is expected to own.

sectionTitle: The AI Fluency 4Ds & Knowing Your Boundary
question: A user runs into a task that clearly requires custom technical implementation they are not equipped to build themselves. What is the appropriate, boundary-aware response?

options.A: Attempt a fragile workaround alone rather than involve anyone else
options.B: Escalate the task to the appropriate engineering/technical team rather than attempting a build outside one's expertise
options.C: Ignore the task entirely
options.D: Pretend the task was completed

explanation: Knowing your boundary includes recognizing when to escalate a task to the people with the right technical expertise, rather than attempting a fragile, out-of-scope build alone.
